1.title: Recorded forever
1.text: Quick warning: everything here is recorded forever. So think before you speak. Okay. This is Bit, and this is reinforcement learning. Let's start with the simplest part.

1.title: What you already know
1.text: You know machine learning, right? Supervised: you have X, you have Y, and you look for a function from X to Y. Unsupervised: you only have X, and you look for structure. Clusters, anomalies. What do they have in common? The data was there in advance. And the learning was passive, like a scientist watching nature. With me so far?

1.title: How does a kid learn?
1.text: Now forget computers. How does a kid learn? Show him a thousand pictures of cats and dogs, and he still doesn't know what's good or bad. He needs feedback. Here's a boiling pot. Bit touches it. Ouch! Pulls back. And never does that again. Did Bit have data in advance? No. Bit started with nothing.

1.title: Why learn on the way?
1.text: Why learn along the way, and not at the end? If Bit only learned at the end, it would keep touching the pot, over and over, until the statistics kick in. By then, evolutionarily, Bit is toast. So we learn on the way, from rewards and punishments. That's reinforcement learning.

1.title: Two differences
1.text: Two things make it different. One: the data arrives along the way. Bit acts, the world answers with what Bit sees and a reward, Bit scribbles it down, and tries again. Two, and this is the important one: the learning is active. What Bit learns changes what data Bit gets next. Bit avoids the pot, so it never samples the pot again. Bit just shaped its own future data. Cool?

1.title: Isn't that just a loss function?
1.text: Isn't that just a loss function? Great question. How many forests do you burn before a supervised model learns that burning forests is bad? Better to catch the signal in the middle, not at the end.

1.title: Chase the total
1.text: And Bit doesn't chase the next reward. It chases the total. Grab every shiny pebble, and the gate shuts behind you. Skip them, and you reach the big star.

1.title: Learn, decide, reach goals
1.text: There are many definitions of intelligence. One I like: the ability to learn, make decisions, and reach goals. Supervised and unsupervised learning don't make decisions. Bit does.

1.title: A bit of history
1.text: A bit of history. The industrial revolution automated our muscles. The digital revolution automated memory and math. My vote for the software that changed humanity the most? Excel. Now we're automating decisions. Every AI wave promises us the Terminator. Let's see if we get there this time.

1.title: The big question
1.text: So, two things to remember. In reinforcement learning, the data arrives along the way, and your choices shape your data. With me so far? Next time: is every goal really just… stars?

2.title: Is every goal just stars?
2.text: Last time, Bit got the big star, and I left you with a question. Is every goal really just… stars? Today we answer it. Kind of.

2.title: The reward hypothesis
2.text: If you take one slide from this whole course, take this one. The reward hypothesis: any goal can be written as maximising one number, the total reward. And notice the word I'm stressing: hypothesis. It's an assumption. No proof, no guarantee. I'll say it thirty times, and then thirty more. Without it, we don't know how to work. So we take it, right or wrong. And notice: the reward is a scalar. One number per step, not a list.

2.title: Rewards in the wild
2.text: Does it feel right? Let's check. Chess: plus one for a win, minus one for a loss. Flying a helicopter: time in the air. Managing a portfolio: more money, less risk. A walking robot: distance? Speed? Not falling over? Maybe all three. Each goal is one circle, but the number behind it can hide a lot of choices. And if your goal really can't be written as a sum of rewards? Then RL won't work well. Find something better, write a good paper, and put me on it.

2.title: Writing the reward is an art
2.text: In RL I'll show you lots of science: formulas, proofs, the works. One thing isn't science. It's art: writing the reward. Watch. I reward Bit for every star he touches. So Bit finds one star and taps it. Forever. Technically, perfect. Okay, I reward distance walked instead. Bit walks in circles. Very far. Going nowhere. So: plus ten for reaching the star, and minus one for every step. Quick lesson in rewards: want something to happen, make it positive. Want to avoid it, make it negative. Now the fastest route wins. Bit was never wrong. My reward was. Writing the reward is where most of the funny bugs in RL come from. You'll see plenty this season.

2.title: Reward vs. loss
2.text: If you know supervised learning: reward is your loss, flipped. There you minimise, here you maximise. And reward isn't a property of the world. A robot vacuum leaves less dust. Is less dust physically good? No. That's us, interpreting. The reward is a number we put on top of the world. Observations and actions belong to the world. The reward is our interpretation, sitting outside it.

2.title: The return
2.text: Now, what Bit actually chases: the sum of all the rewards from now on. We call it the return, G. G for goal. Easy to remember. Notice it starts from now. Philosophically: don't cry over spilt milk. What you did so far, you can't change. The goal is from here on. And as Bit moves on, the return moves with him. It's always measured from wherever he stands.

2.title: Value: the return you expect
2.text: Quick question: standing here, does Bit know his return? No! The future hasn't happened yet. So we use the next best thing: the value of a spot, the return Bit expects from there. Why expects? Because the world can be random. Chess has no dice. Backgammon does. Same move, different outcomes. Look at this board: all your pieces, against one sad king in the middle. High value. You can feel it. For the other side? Very low. And look: the value talks about states. The actions are hiding inside the future rewards.

2.title: Now or later?
2.text: Now it gets interesting. Bit's fuel is running low. Straight ahead: three easy stars. To the left: a fuel station, and no stars at all. The greedy move grabs the stars, and runs dry two steps later. The detour costs stars now, and wins more later. That's value: not what you get now, but everything you can expect from here.

2.title: Value of an action: q
2.text: One more. A dungeon game. Bit stands on a tile: gold ahead, and lava on both sides. What's this tile worth? Good? Bad? Honestly, weird. So we ask a better question: how good is this tile, together with the move I'm about to make? This tile plus gold: very high. This tile plus lava: very low. That's the action value, q. q for quality. Value asks: how good is this place? q asks: how good is this place, if I do this?

2.title: Look around the corner: Bellman
2.text: Last trick. The return is the next reward, plus the return after it. So value is: reward now, plus the value of where you land. Instead of predicting the whole game, look only around the corner. Much friendlier. One step at a time: the reward you're about to get, plus a guess for everything after. We'll be back to this. It has a name: the Bellman equation. With me so far? Next time: what does Bit actually see?

3.title: Does the robot see the room?
3.text: Quick quiz. A robot vacuum has a camera. Does it see the whole room? No. It sees a slice. The room is the world. The slice is what the robot gets. That gap is this whole episode. And it's not just robots. Right now, you see a slice of this room, not the whole building.

3.title: State vs. observation
3.text: The environment state is everything true about the world: every star, every rock, every gust of wind. Bit doesn't get that. Bit gets an observation. Usually much smaller, and often missing exactly the part you need. Even Bit has a state of his own. A vacuum cleans the room, and its battery drops. The action changed the world, and the agent.

3.title: History
3.text: So what does Bit have? His history. The first observation, the action he took, the reward he got. Then the next observation, and so on. Everything, up to right now. Problem: it never stops growing. Long day, very long ribbon. History is the raw material. Everything Bit knows, he has to build from it.

3.title: Fully observable worlds
3.text: For most of this course, we'll make a simplifying assumption: what you observe is the state. In chess, that's true. You look at the board, and the board is the whole game. In symbols: the state S t equals the observation O t. We call that fully observable. With real robots and real sensors? Almost never. We'll keep that assumption for most of the course, and drop it later on.

3.title: Markov
3.text: Now, a word you'll hear a lot: Markov. By the way, Markov is a surname. A Markov process says one simple thing: I remember nothing. What happens next depends only on where I am now, not on how I got here. Formally: the chance of the next state and reward, given the state, is the same as given the whole history. Is the weather Markov? Sunny today says something about tomorrow. But not everything. Seasons! Without the history, you'll be wrong at some point. So not everything is Markov. But it's usually a not-bad approximation. And the test is simple: if adding more history doesn't help, the state is Markov. Then you can throw the history away. Good news for your memory, and your computer's. Careful: Markov doesn't mean the state holds everything. It means more history wouldn't help.

3.title: When Markov breaks
3.text: Let's see it break. Bit is in a maze, and he only sees the three by three squares around him. Here, he sees this. And here, on the other side of the maze, exactly the same thing. But here, the exit is down. And here, it's up. If Bit decides on the observation alone, he must make the same move in both. Mathematically, no choice. So he'll be wrong in one of them. Every time. And a smarter policy doesn't fix it. The information simply isn't in the observation.

3.title: The fix: remember
3.text: The fix: Bit remembers where he came from. He keeps a small state card, and updates it every step: old state, last action, reward and new observation give the new state. Now the two spots look different, and the symmetry breaks. And here's the magic: the card from one step ago already carried what mattered from thirty steps ago. Remember I said recursion comes back? It comes back a lot. That update function, u, is something we design, or something Bit learns.

3.title: Why not just observations?
3.text: Why bother? Why not just work with observations? Because if all our math lives in how the robot sees the world, we get very good at the robot's view, not at the world. We're turning a subjective truth into an objective one. Sometimes that's not easy.

3.title: Partially observable
3.text: When Bit can't see the full state, we call the problem partially observable. A poker player only sees the public cards. A robot's camera isn't told where the robot is. The world can still be Markov. Bit just doesn't know it yet. He discovers it along the way. Later in the course we'll come back to this properly. For now, the assumption stays.

3.title: Two things to remember
3.text: So, two things to remember. Bit doesn't act on the world as it is. He acts on his state: what he built from what he saw. And if that state is good, the past can go. Cool? And every other gadget lives on that state. Policy, value, model: all of them. Next time, we open Bit up and see what's inside.

4.title: Opening the hatch
4.text: Today we open Bit up. Don't worry, it's a cute hatch. Inside an agent there are up to three gadgets. A policy, a value function, and a model.

4.title: The policy
4.text: First, the policy: a map from state to action. Given where I am, what do I do? We write it pi. Don't ask me why. P was already taken, for probabilities. A deterministic policy is a compass needle: one state, one move. A stochastic policy is a spinner: one state, a probability for each move, and you sample. In code, a stochastic policy is just a table of probabilities: for each state, one per action. Then you sample.

4.title: The value function
4.text: Second, the value function: how good is this state? But careful: good for whom? Give the same chess position to a beginner and to a grandmaster. The value isn't the same. Value always depends on the policy that keeps playing from there. Same board, same pieces. Different player, different future.

4.title: The discount, γ
4.text: And a new dial: the discount, gamma, between zero and one. Every step further into the future, a reward is multiplied by gamma once more. It shrinks exponentially. Gamma equals one: the plain sum from last time. Gamma equals zero: only the next reward counts. That's a greedy algorithm! So RL literally extends greedy algorithms. Nice, no? Care only about now? Low gamma. Need to plan far ahead? High gamma, like 0.99. Gamma sets the effective horizon: roughly how many steps ahead Bit really cares about.

4.title: Bellman, with γ
4.text: With gamma, last time's recursion becomes: value is reward now, plus gamma times the value of where you land. That's the Bellman equation. Fun fact: it doesn't come from RL at all. It comes from optimisation theory. We stole it. And for the best possible value, the same function sits on both sides. If a value keeps changing every time you visit it, you're not at the optimum yet.

4.title: The model
4.text: Third gadget: the model. Until now we had sensible names. Here we gave up: the prediction model is just, the model. It predicts what the world does next: the next state, and the next reward. In chess, you move the knight and you know the next board. Easy, for you. A computer holding the board as a list of numbers needs someone to compute it. That's the model. In backgammon, the dice make the next board a distribution, so the model predicts probabilities, not one board. And rewards can be nasty: the square root of the distance, times the chance you're spotted, minus the weather outside. Good luck. One important thing: a model doesn't act. Bit still has to think with it. That's called planning. And every model is a guess. A good guess saves a lot of real-world mistakes.

4.title: All three on one maze
4.text: Let's watch all three on one maze. Minus one for every step, so the shortest path wins. The policy: an arrow in every cell. Quiz: this cell, does Bit ever reach it? No. So does its arrow matter? No! So even this toy maze has a huge number of optimal policies: any arrow, in every cell Bit never visits. The value: the number of steps to the goal, as a negative number. Standing on minus eight, where do you go? Minus seven, or minus nine? Minus seven! Always step to the highest value you can reach. That simple rule gives you the policy. Policy and value are two views of one problem: one in actions, one in states. From the values you can rebuild the arrows, and from the arrows, the values. Two perspectives, same problem. And the model: Bit's own map of the walls, with a minus one stamped on each cell. These numbers only make sense because the reward is minus one per step. Change the reward, and every number changes.

4.title: Kinds of agents
4.text: So different agents just switch on different gadgets. Value-based: keep the values, and read the policy off them. It doesn't get a policy. It derives one. Policy-based: learn the policy directly. Actor-critic: both. Spoiler: it usually works best. And separately: model-free, learning only from experience, or model-based, building a model and using it. We'll meet every one of these this season, some of them in deep-learning form.

4.title: Three gadgets
4.text: So, three gadgets. The policy picks. The value judges. The model imagines. Find them, and Bit can act. Approximate them well, and he can act well, even in huge worlds. With me so far? Next time: the four problems the whole season solves.

5.title: Zooming out
5.text: Last episode of module one! Let's zoom out. Every RL problem hides two very different problems. Two problems, and two ways to solve them. That makes four squares.

5.title: Prediction vs. control
5.text: Prediction: given a way of acting, how good is the future? You evaluate. Control: find the best way of acting. You optimise. They're tied together. The best policy has the best values, and the best values give you the best policy. And a question to think about: if we could predict everything, would we need anything else? And prediction is built in: every definition we wrote looks at future rewards. Two problems, one goal. Who remembers which? Maximise the total reward.

5.title: A classic gridworld
5.text: Here's a classic gridworld. Bump into a wall: minus one. Step on A: plus ten, and you jump to A prime. Step on B: plus five, and you land on B prime. Prediction first: if Bit wanders at random, what's each square worth? Near the walls, negative. Around A, high, even though A throws you away. Look at A itself: worth eight point eight, less than its ten. You jump to A prime, right next to a wall. B is worth five point three, more than its five: B prime lands you in the open. Now control: what's the best Bit can possibly do? Every square gets better, and the arrows head for A. Ten beats five, even with the long walk back. Notice: the best values beat the random ones everywhere. That's what good acting buys you.

5.title: Learning vs. planning
5.text: The second split: learning versus planning. A robot vacuum enters a new room. How can it plan a route if it doesn't know the room? So first, it drives around and discovers the room. That's learning: interacting with an unknown world. Then it goes home, sits, and plans the best route in its head. That's planning: thinking with a model, no new interaction. Ants do it too: wander until one finds food, then the whole colony forms a line. Learn, plan, learn, plan. In the math, learning and planning sit together. In practice, you have to explore the space, and plan over it.

5.title: The two-by-two map
5.text: Put it together and you get a two by two map: predict or control, by learn or plan. Predict while learning: how good is my way of acting, from experience. Control while planning: the best way, from a model. And the two in between. The rest of the season fills in these four squares.

5.title: Four functions
5.text: And to fill them, we need just four functions. Policy: state to action. Value: state to a number. Model: the next state and reward. And state update: from observations to a state. Find these four, and you've solved the problem. The whole course asks one question: what kinds of solutions for them are good? Each of the four is just a function. Tables, formulas, neural networks: all fair game. Deep learning, for example, can fill one of them, or several. An Atari agent might use a network just to turn pixels into numbers. Rules unknown, no answer key. Just joystick moves, pixels, and a score. Learning directly from play.

5.title: When to pick RL
5.text: So when should you pick RL at all? Say you trained a sales model for a shop. It works great for two months. Then something very sad happens: a competitor opens two shops away. The world changed under the model's feet. That's concept drift, and it's more common than you'd think. RL keeps learning while it runs, so it can keep up. Supervised learning splits fit and predict. RL doesn't have to. It learns while it acts. A world that changes, and decisions in a sequence. That's where RL shines. And sometimes it's spectacular: robots that learn to walk, run and jump, with nobody writing down the steps.

5.title: Module one, done
5.text: Module one, done. That's most of the definitions; from here, fewer new words and more algorithms. Next stop: a beach full of slot machines. Explore, or exploit? One state, many choices: the cleanest place to watch exploration happen.

6.title: Explore, then exploit
6.text: Module two! And we start with something you already do every day. You want to learn a new field. So you google, read the first site, then the third, a bit here, a bit there. Slowly you learn the right words, and who to read. That's exploration: gathering knowledge. Then you use what you learned to write your paper. That's exploitation: using knowledge to decide well. Usually you explore first, then exploit. But it's not that linear: you go back and forth. Or ants. I know watching ants is something you do a lot in your day. They leave the nest and wander, more or less at random, until one finds food. She goes back, tells her friends, and you get the line. That line is exploitation of new knowledge.

6.title: A world with one state
6.text: To study this, we simplify the world to a single state. With one state, does order matter? No. Nothing I did yesterday changes today. Actions still give rewards. They just don't move us anywhere. I know, I said RL is for sequences of decisions. One state removes that, on purpose. We'll fill the gap later.

6.title: The bandit
6.text: Long, long ago, in a land far away, there was a machine with many handles. At fairs and theatres, you'd pull a handle and get a prize, or a punishment. It was dressed up as a bandit. Many arms, one bandit: the multi-armed bandit. Pull a handle, let it go. The machine doesn't change. One state. Perfect for us. Fun fact: the bandit problem is older than RL itself.

6.title: A circus thought experiment
6.text: Thought experiment. I run a circus, which isn't far from my reality right now. Bit comes to win lots of money. My bandit has ten handles. Bit starts by pulling each handle once. Smart: he knows nothing, so he explores. Then he keeps pulling the one that paid the most. Is he sure it's the best? No! One pull is noise. Maybe a quiet handle pays a fortune once every hundred pulls. And notice: the goal isn't just to find the best handle. It's to win the most money along the way.

6.title: Expected reward
6.text: So what are we really after? The expected reward of each handle. We call it q of a. Why expected? Pull the same handle again and again, and the average settles on it. That's the law of large numbers. Bit can't know q. But he can estimate it: the average reward he got from that handle. A capital Q. And we count how many times Bit pulled each handle: N of a. Pulled a handle a hundred times? N is a hundred. The best Bit could ever do? Pull the best handle every single time. That's the optimal value, v star. With one state, the value is just one number per handle. We can drop the s.

6.title: Learning one pull at a time
6.text: And he can update it one pull at a time: new estimate equals old estimate, plus a step times the surprise. Look familiar? It's gradient descent. With a step of one over the number of pulls, the first pull moves you a lot, and the thousandth barely at all. Slower, but stable: at pull one thousand, one crazy value doesn't throw you around. That's the trade-off in the step size: big steps learn fast and shake, small steps learn slowly and stay calm.

6.title: Regret
6.text: Now we need a score for the learner itself. It's called regret. Regret is the gap between the best handle and the handle you actually pulled. Pull the best one: zero regret. Pull a worse one: you pay the difference. Add it up over all your pulls and you get the total regret. Maximising total reward and minimising total regret are the same thing. If you like loss functions: in our world, the loss is called regret. Regret uses something Bit doesn't know: the best handle. So it's a score for us, the designers, not a signal for Bit.

6.title: The tension
6.text: And here's the tension. Exploring raises your regret. We explore because we must, not because it's fun. Exploiting should raise it less. Ideally, not at all. Watch the curve: steep while Bit explores, flatter once he knows. A good learner keeps the steep part short.

6.title: A problem, not an algorithm
6.text: One last thing: the multi-armed bandit is not an algorithm. It's a problem, the simplest RL problem there is. And because it's so simple, it's where nearly every exploration idea gets tried first. Next time, the algorithms, starting with the greediest one. With me so far?

7.title: Greedy
7.text: The simplest algorithm: greedy. Always pull the handle whose estimate is highest. What could go wrong? The best handle pays little on its first pull. Just bad luck. Its estimate drops below an average handle. Greedy never pulls it again. Never. So it never finds out. Stuck forever on the wrong handle, regret grows in a straight line. In the real world, nobody hands you the true expectations. It would be nice. It doesn't happen. Greedy isn't stupid. It's just confident, too early.

7.title: ε-greedy
7.text: So, a small fix. And if you remember one thing from this course, remember this one. Epsilon-greedy. Seriously: the most important algorithm in the course. Most of the time, with probability one minus epsilon, pull the best-looking handle. With probability epsilon, pull any handle at random. That random pull is what saves you from getting stuck. And the random pull can land on the best handle too. With epsilon at 0.1 and ten handles, the best-looking one gets picked 91% of the time. Epsilon is the knob: zero is plain greedy, one is pure chaos.

7.title: Is it perfect?
7.text: Is it perfect? With a constant epsilon, Bit keeps exploring forever, so regret still grows in a straight line. Just a gentler one. Linear sounds bad. But who remembers running times? Linear is really fine. What you'd really like is a big epsilon at the start, that shrinks over time. That's what people do in practice. Can you know the best schedule in advance? Practically, no. You try. And if epsilon shrinks at the right speed, regret can grow much slower than a straight line.

7.title: It's everywhere
7.text: And it's everywhere. Most RL algorithms today have epsilon-greedy somewhere inside. I recently published a paper with epsilon-greedy right inside. Works great. Not because it's clever. Because it's simple, and it works.

7.title: A simulation
7.text: Here's a real simulation: ten handles, two thousand runs, averaged. Greedy settles early, on whatever it found first. Epsilon-greedy keeps learning, and pulls ahead. The exact numbers depend on the problem. The shape is the point.

7.title: Learn the policy directly
7.text: Now a different idea. Instead of estimating values, learn the policy directly. Each handle gets a preference: just a number. A softmax turns the preferences into probabilities. Why? Rewards live on an arbitrary scale. Double them, halve them, I don't care, as long as the order stays. Arbitrary scales are hard to work with. Probabilities, between zero and one, I understand. If you did deep learning: it's the same softmax as in classification. So the policy is the softmax of the preferences. Big preference, big probability.

7.title: Climb the gradient
7.text: Then we climb. Gradient ascent, not descent. Plus, not minus: we're maximising reward, so we walk up the hill. Pull a handle and get a reward. Push that handle's preference up in proportion to the reward, and the others down. Why does this climb the right hill? Picture two handles at fifty-fifty. Shift a little probability to the first: the expected reward changes by how much better the first one is. Handles that pay more climb faster. And the math has a neat trick: this gradient is something you can sample, one pull at a time. It's called the log-likelihood trick, or the REINFORCE trick, from 1992. The price: the steps are noisy. Stochastic gradient ascent.

7.title: Three ways to explore
7.text: So: greedy gets stuck. Epsilon-greedy explores on purpose. Gradient bandits learn the policy itself. Three ways to explore: none at all, at random, or by following the gradient of your own policy. And all three share one loop: pull, observe, update. Only the update changes. Next time: can we explore smarter than a coin flip? Cool?

8.title: Luck or uncertainty?
8.text: Three handles, and Bit's beliefs about each one. Red looks best on average. Green is lower, but very uncertain. If you want the highest expected reward right now, you pick red. That's the theory so far. Now suppose Bit is famously lucky. Wakes up, wins the lottery, walks into the bakery right as the croissants come out of the oven. Now which one? The wide green one: it might be amazing. We can't build on luck. But we can build on uncertainty. Why do we keep talking about expectations? Sample enough, and you get close to them. And luck is not a strategy.

8.title: Optimism
8.text: The idea is called optimism in the face of uncertainty. Don't pick what looks great. Pick what could be great. For each handle, take the estimate, plus a bonus for how unsure you are. An upper confidence bound. Pulled a lot: small bonus. Barely pulled: big bonus. So a handle wins either because it's good, or because we don't know it well yet. Does the bonus ever reach zero? Not necessarily. The world's own randomness never goes away. Notice what changed: we're not maximising the estimate anymore. We're maximising an upper bound on

8.title: Hoeffding's inequality
8.text: it. Just saying be optimistic is nice. Let's do better than nice. Hoeffding's inequality: the chance that your average plus the bonus is still below the truth shrinks exponentially, in the number of pulls, and in the bonus squared. Choose how small that chance should be, solve for the bonus, and you get a formula: the square root of the log of time, over twice the number of pulls. Time ticks on its own, and the number of pulls you control. So you can ask: how many pulls until I'm this sure? Say you want to be within 0.1, after a thousand steps. You need about 350 pulls of that handle. Within 0.01? About 35,000. Precision is expensive. And as time goes on, we keep shrinking the chance of being wrong: one over t.

8.title: The UCB algorithm
8.text: Put it together: the UCB algorithm. Pull the handle with the highest estimate plus bonus, scaled by a constant, c. With c equal to the square root of two, the regret grows only logarithmically. Logarithmic! Steep while you explore, almost flat once you know. Why does it work? Regret is the gap of each handle, times how often you pulled it. UCB makes sure that for every handle, either the gap is small, or the count is small. Big gap, few pulls. That's the whole trick. So UCB explores a lot at first, then less and less, without anyone setting a

8.title: Can anyone do better?
8.text: schedule. Can anyone do better? Lai and Robbins proved that, in the long run, no algorithm beats logarithmic regret. Nice, and not nice. You're guaranteed never to be perfect. But you know your boundaries. The bound depends on how close the handles are. Similar handles are hard to tell apart, and cost more regret.

8.title: A simulation
8.text: Same simulation as last time. Epsilon-greedy: a straight line. UCB: it bends, and flattens. Same ten handles, same two thousand runs. Only the algorithm changed.

8.title: In practice
8.text: By the way, plain greedy isn't a real method. Nobody uses it. And should you add UCB to your agent? You can't know in advance. Try it with and without. One more variant: if Bit keeps a belief for each handle, he can use the belief's spread as the bonus. Mean plus c times the spread. Greedy, epsilon-greedy, UCB: each is a different answer to the same question. How much do I explore?

8.title: Try what might be great
8.text: So: try what might be great, not just what looks great. Optimism isn't wishful thinking. It's a bonus with a proof. Next time: what if Bit keeps a whole belief instead of one number? With me so far?

9.title: A belief, not a number
9.text: So far, Bit kept one number per handle: his best guess. Today he keeps a belief. Not what the value is, but how much he believes in each possible value. If Bit believes it's 8 with 99% confidence, then practically, it's 8. A distribution over distributions. I know, it's confusing. Stay with me. Why bother? Because one number throws away how sure you are. A belief keeps it.

9.title: Win or lose: the Beta belief
9.text: Simplest case: each handle either pays one, or nothing. Win or lose. Before any pull, Bit knows nothing, so his belief is flat: every win rate from zero to one is equally likely. Win: the belief leans right. Win again: further right. Then lose, lose. If he just counted, two and two, it would look like he's back at the start. But the belief remembers. It's now a hump around one half. He knows more than when he began. This curve is called a Beta distribution. Count the wins, count the losses, and that's all you need to keep. Flat at the start is Beta one, one. Two wins and two losses later: Beta three, three. And if you're so smart that you know the right belief from the start? Start there. Everything converges much faster. Four pulls, two wins: a wide hump. Four hundred pulls, two hundred wins: a narrow spike. Same average, very different certainty.

9.title: A confession about the real world
9.text: And a confession about the real world. Outside of math, in engineering, in physics, nobody ever hands you the true distribution. We estimate it from what we observe. A belief is honest about that. And Beta is the natural belief for win-or-lose: a rate between zero and one.

9.title: Thompson sampling
9.text: Now the algorithm: Thompson sampling. It's old: 1933, older than most of computer science. Each round, every handle draws one random guess from its own belief. Bit pulls the handle with the highest guess, sees the result, and updates that belief. So a handle gets pulled about as often as Bit believes it's the best one. That's called probability matching. Unsure handles draw wild guesses, so they get tried. Handles known to be bad almost never win the draw. And for win-or-lose bandits, it matches the Lai and Robbins bound. It's optimal. No bonus to tune, no epsilon to schedule. The uncertainty does the exploring.

9.title: Watch it learn
9.text: Watch the beliefs. The best handle's curve gets narrow and tall, and wins almost every draw. Same kind of simulation: a win-or-lose bandit, two thousand runs. UCB bends. Thompson sampling bends even lower. Different paths, same lesson: explore where you're unsure, exploit where you're sure. And beliefs only narrow where Bit pulls. The bad handles stay a bit uncertain, and that's fine. They're bad.

9.title: The information state
9.text: One more idea, to close the module. We said a bandit has one state. But what Bit knows keeps changing. So treat his knowledge as part of the state: the wins and losses of every handle. Each pull moves him to a new information state. Even in a bandit, actions affect the future, through learning. Now it's a full decision problem, and you can plan to explore. It's called Bayes-adaptive RL. Optimal, in theory. Unwieldy, in practice. Every pull is worth what it pays, plus what it teaches. Planning to explore puts a price on the teaching. That's why it's rarely used directly. But it tells you what exploration is worth.

9.title: Module two, done
9.text: Two lectures in, and you already have algorithms that provably find the best handle, with only logarithmic regret along the way. That some of them would finish after the universe collapses into itself? That's another conversation. Because a bandit has one state, and real problems have many. In chess, I take your queen, and on the next move, you checkmate me. Next module: states, and consequences. So, module two in one line: explore where you're unsure, exploit where you're sure. With me so far? See you in module three.

10.title: From one state to many
10.text: Welcome back. About three hundred million years have passed since the last episode. Roughly. Last module, Bit lived in a world with one state: a row of slot machines. Pull, get paid, pull again. Nothing he did changed the world. Real problems aren't like that. In chess, I take your queen, and on the next move you checkmate me. Today: many states, and consequences.

10.title: Markov
10.text: First, a name you'll hear a lot: Markov. And by the way, Markov is a surname. It's a person, not a thing. A Markov chain is a process with no memory. To predict what comes next, the present is enough. Knowing the whole history doesn't make the prediction any better. Is the weather Markov? Not really. Today's weather alone won't tell you that winter is coming. The season matters. Chess? Yes. Give me the board, and I don't care how you got there. Quick quiz. Let's find a victim. A card game where you only see your own hand. Markov? Not from your seat. Which cards were already played tells you a lot. The history matters. A Markov chain, you watch. Things happen to you, and you just observe. A Markov decision process, you act. Your choices change what happens next. That's the difference.

10.title: The MDP
10.text: So, formally, an MDP is a few things together. S: the set of all the states. A: the set of all the actions. p: the dynamics, the probability of landing in each next state, with each reward, after an action. And γ, the discount. We'll get to it in a minute. In chess, S is every legal board, and A is every legal move. Both are enormous. That problem will follow us all season. So an MDP is the rules of the game. The agent's job is to play it well.

10.title: Why probabilities?
10.text: Why probabilities? Picture a remote-controlled robot arm. You tell it: lift ten degrees. It lifts nine. The motor, the sensor, the control loop… infinite reasons. So the same action doesn't always land in the same place. Now, if I knew p perfectly, could I play perfectly? In principle, yes. Think two hundred moves ahead, in your head. Not feasible for big games. But in principle, p is everything. p is the dynamics. And we'll assume p never changes. If it does, the rules change under your feet. That's called concept drift. No concept drift in this course. Want concept drift? Do a PhD.

10.title: The can-collecting robot
10.text: An example. A robot that collects soda cans. Its battery is either high or low. Two states. With a high battery, it can search for cans, or wait for someone to bring one. With a low battery, it can also go back and recharge. And if it searches on low, it might run flat and need rescuing. Searching pays more than waiting. Rescues cost a lot. Those numbers are the reward, and we choose them. Now, a game. What if waiting paid more than searching? The best strategy is… wait. Forever. Is that what you want from a cleaning robot? Same lesson as before: define the reward properly. And notice: recharging now means more cleaning later. Today's choice changes tomorrow's options. That's what sequential means.

10.title: The return and the discount
10.text: So what is Bit after now? The return: the sum of the rewards from here on. Problem: if Bit gets one point every step, forever, the sum is infinity. Every policy that never stops looks the same. Also, honestly? We don't care that much about what happens in a thousand years. So we discount. Each step further away, multiply by γ, a number between zero and one. Now the sum is finite. Say every reward is at most 10. Then the return is at most 10 over one minus γ. With γ at 0.9: 100. γ near one: Bit looks far ahead. γ near zero: he looks only at the next step. γ equals zero: pure greed. Think of it like the horizon at sea. You know there's more out there, it just doesn't bother you. With γ at point nine, that horizon is about ten steps. At point nine nine, about a hundred.

10.title: Why discount?
10.text: Why else discount? Money now is worth more than money later: it earns interest. The future is uncertain, and our model of it is never perfect. People and animals prefer rewards sooner, too. There are other options, like the average reward per step. But the discounted return is the classic default. Average reward is handy for tasks that never end, like a server that runs forever. Does γ actually help your problem? Run it once with γ and once without. Congratulations, you just got a project idea.

10.title: What Bit will collect
10.text: One last thing. The return at time t isn't what Bit collected. It's what he will collect, from now on. It's in the future, so it's random. That's why next time we'll talk about its expected value. So, an MDP: states, actions, dynamics, rewards, and a discount. The whole sequential world in one tuple. Next: what does it mean for a policy to be the best? With me so far?

11.title: The policy
11.text: We all gathered here today for one reason: to find the policy. A policy, π, tells Bit what to do in every state. Tell me what the world looks like, and I'll tell you what to do in it. It can be fixed, one action per state, or random, a probability for each action. And remember the duality from module one: know the values, and you know how to act. Know the policy, and you can work out its values.

11.title: Values
11.text: Now, the value of a state, under a policy: the return Bit expects, starting there and following π. Notice the π in there. We now live inside a context: the policy. Every reward in the return comes from an action, and every action comes from the policy. Change the policy, change the value. Same state, two policies, two different values. A value always belongs to a policy. And q, the value of an action: take this action first, and then follow π. v answers: how good is it to be here? q answers: how good is it to do this, here?

11.title: Which policy is better?
11.text: Okay. So what's a better policy? If I say I'm better than you, I have to say better at what. We need an order. You can't just compare two policies. But each policy has a value, and values are numbers. So: π is at least as good as π prime if its value is at least as high in every single state. Every. A hundred million states, better in all of them but one, worse in one? Not better. Very strict. And some pairs of policies can't be compared at all. That's fine. Think of two students. One is better at maths, the other at history. Who's the better student? Depends who's asking.

11.title: The promise
11.text: Why bother with such a strict order? Because it buys us a promise. Each improvement only goes up. And values can't go up forever: rewards are bounded, so the return is bounded. Something that only goes up, and is bounded, converges. That's first-year calculus. And the theorem: there's always an optimal policy, π star, at least as good as every other policy, in every state. There may be several. They all share the same values: v star and q star. Two routes home of exactly the same length? Both optimal. Same value, different policies. This is the only course that makes you good promises. What did computer vision promise you? A headache, and a crazy GPU bill.

11.title: Greedy on q*
11.text: And if someone hands you q star, acting is easy. In every state, pick the action with the highest q star. That's an optimal policy. Done. So finding the best behaviour and finding the best values are the same problem, seen from two sides. That's why, from now on, we'll chase values. Get the values right, and the policy comes for free.

11.title: The Bellman equation
11.text: Now, the most basic equation in RL. We'll meet it all the time from now on: the Bellman equation. The value of a state is the reward you get now, plus γ times the value of where you land. Averaged over what π picks, and over where p sends you. Read it out loud once. It's the sentence this whole course is built on. It's recursive: a value, defined by other values. One step, then let the next state worry about the rest. Let's check one. Next episode we'll meet a grid where a square next to the exit is worth minus fourteen. Its four neighbours average out to minus thirteen. Minus one for the step: minus fourteen. Bellman holds. Same for q: the reward now, plus γ times the value of the next state and the next action.

11.title: Bellman optimality
11.text: And for the best policy, there's a twist. Instead of averaging over the actions, take the best one. v star of a state is the max over actions: reward now, plus γ times v star of where you land. That's the Bellman optimality equation. In plain words: the best you can do from here is the best first step, followed by the best you can do from there. That max makes it non-linear. Remember that. It'll matter next episode. So from now on: the expectation equation to evaluate, and the optimality equation to find the

11.title: A tiny example
11.text: best. A tiny example. From the start, going left pays one point, and the game ends. Going right pays nothing now, but leads to a state that pays five. With γ at point nine, right is worth four and a half. Bigger than one. Go right. With γ at point one, right is worth half a point. Now left wins. Same world, different γ, different best policy. That's Bellman doing its job: today's reward, plus the discounted best of tomorrow. And with γ equal to one? Right is worth five. No contest.

11.title: Three words
11.text: So what are we really trying to maximise? Three words. Expected. Cumulative. Reward. Repeat after me. Values tell you how good things are. The order tells you which policy is better. Bellman ties it all together. A promise: an optimal policy always exists. A recipe: be greedy on q star. A tool: Bellman. Next time: we actually solve these equations. Once with a matrix, and once with sweeps. With me so far?

12.title: Prediction and control
12.text: Last time, we wrote the Bellman equation. Today we solve it. There are two problems. Prediction: here's a policy, how good is it? That's also called policy evaluation. Control: find the best policy. Given this treatment protocol, or this trading strategy, what's my expected return? That's prediction. Which one should I use? That's control. Prediction is the inner loop. Control is what we actually want.

12.title: The matrix form
12.text: Start with prediction. For a fixed policy, the Bellman equation is linear. Stack all the values into one vector. The rewards into another. The transitions into a matrix. Then v equals r, plus γ times P times v. One line. Move things around, and v is the inverse of one minus γ P, times r. Done! Right? For a small problem, that really is the answer. Exact, in one shot. Write it for three states, and you could solve it by hand. Try it. It's a nice exercise.

12.title: What it costs
12.text: Computer science people will tell you: matrix inversion is n cubed. Polynomial. That's fine. Two thousand states: eight billion operations. A few seconds. Heavy, but feasible. A million states: ten to the eighteen operations. On one core doing a few billion a second, that's about ten years. And chess has far, far more than a million states. And for control, the Bellman optimality equation has a max in it. Not linear. No matrix trick at all. Polynomial, it turns out, isn't the same as practical.

12.title: Dynamic programming
12.text: So we need iterative methods. And the classic family is called dynamic programming. Where does the name come from? Richard Bellman, the same Bellman. Honestly, I always forget his first name is Richard. He later said that the nineteen fifties were not good years for mathematical research. So he picked a name that didn't sound like maths. And people say dynamic programming means storing computations so you don't repeat them. That's a side effect of programming. Dynamic programming has one property: break a problem into a smaller problem, again and again, until you reach one you can solve directly. And the Bellman equation is already built that way: the value of a state is the reward now, plus a smaller problem: the value of the next state. And it assumes we know the MDP perfectly. p, the rewards, everything. For now, we do.

12.title: Turn = into ←
12.text: Here's the trick. Take the Bellman equation, and turn the equals sign into an update. Value at step k plus one: the reward, plus γ times the value at step k of where you land. Start with all zeros. Sweep over every state. Then sweep again, using the new values. And again. Stop when the values stop moving, or when they change by less than some small number. That's iterative policy evaluation. In code: two arrays, old values and new values. Every state reads the old ones and writes a new one. Swap, and repeat. There's another way: one array, overwritten as you go. We'll get to it in two episodes.

12.title: Watching it sweep
12.text: Let's watch it. A four by four grid. Two corners are exits. Every step costs one point. The policy: totally random. Up, down, left, right, a quarter each. Sweep zero: all zeros. Bit has no preferences at all. Sweep one: every square is minus one. One step costs one. Sweep two: the squares next to an exit are at minus one point seven five. The others at minus two. Sweep three: minus two point four, minus two point nine, minus three. It keeps going. Keep sweeping, and it settles: minus fourteen next to the exits, minus twenty-two in the far corners. A random walker takes a long time to get out. And that minus fourteen from last episode? Here it is. Bellman, checked.

12.title: The arrows
12.text: Now, a trick. In each square, draw an arrow toward the best neighbour. At sweep zero, every direction ties. Nothing to choose. At sweep three, the arrows already point the shortest way home. The optimal policy. After three sweeps! Could we have stopped there? No. From inside, there's no way to know the arrows won't change again. The values were still far from the truth. Only the order happened to be right. Notice what mattered: not the numbers themselves, only their order. Minus three or minus twenty-two, the arrows are the same. The numbers tell you how long a random walker suffers. The arrows tell you what a smart walker should do. Different questions. If you can invent an order on policies that tells you when to stop early, come talk to me. We'll write a Nature paper.

12.title: Matrix or sweeps
12.text: So now we can evaluate any policy: with a matrix if it's small, with sweeps if it's not. And the arrows trick, acting greedily on the values, is the seed of the next idea. Each sweep touches every state, every action and every next state. Remember that cost. Prediction, solved. Now let's use it for control. Next time: evaluate, improve, evaluate, improve. Policy iteration, and a car rental business. With me so far?

13.title: Check, improve
13.text: Do you know how ABS brakes work? They measure the wheels, then act so the car doesn't skid. Measure, act, measure, act. Classic control engineering. And reinforcement learning borrowed exactly that loop. Your thermostat does it too. Measure the room, switch the heating, measure again. Check. Improve. Check. Improve. Check. Improve. Until it doesn't improve anymore.

13.title: Greedy improvement
13.text: We already know how to check: policy evaluation. Now, how to improve. In every state, look at q of π: the value of each action, if afterwards you follow your old policy. Pick the action with the highest q. That's the new policy. π prime is the arg max of q π. Don't let the math scare you. It says: given what you know now, do what looks best. A real example, from the problem we'll see in a minute. In one state, under the old lazy policy, doing nothing is worth five hundred nineteen dollars. Moving five cars is worth five hundred forty-one. So the new policy moves five. That's all improvement is.

13.title: Why it can't get worse
13.text: Why can't this make things worse? In each state, the greedy action is at least as good as what the old policy did. Take it once, then follow the old policy: no worse. Take it again at the next step: still no worse. Unroll it all the way. So the new policy's value is at least the old one's, in every state. Our strict order, satisfied. Better in every state: exactly the order from two episodes ago. And if the policy stops changing? Then the values satisfy the Bellman optimality equation. You're optimal. One warning. This greedy is not the greedy from bandits. There, greedy meant no exploration. Here, it's a step in the space of policies. Different job.

13.title: Policy iteration
13.text: Put it together: policy iteration. Start with any policy. I'd be happy if you started somewhere good. But I have no idea how to promise you that. Evaluate it. Act greedily on the values. That's a new policy. Evaluate it. Improve again. Each new policy makes the old values a bit wrong. So we evaluate again. It zigzags, and lands on the optimal values, and the optimal policy. How many rounds does it take? Usually, surprisingly few.

13.title: Jack's car rental
13.text: A real example: Jack's car rental. Jack runs two locations, and each holds up to twenty cars. Every car rented earns ten dollars. Customers arrive at random: about three a day at the first place, four at the second. Returns are random too: about three a day at the first, two at the second. Random arrivals like these follow a Poisson distribution. Three on average. Sometimes none, sometimes eight. Overnight, Jack can move up to five cars between the locations, at two dollars a car. And γ is point nine. The state: how many cars at each place. Twenty-one times twenty-one: four hundred forty-one states. And eleven possible moves in each, from five one way to five the other. Small enough for dynamic programming. The question: how many cars to move tonight, in each of those states?

13.title: Our run
13.text: We ran it. Start with the lazy policy: never move anything. Evaluate, improve: the first new policy already moves cars toward the busier location. Again, and again. The border between moving and not moving gets sharper each time. After four improvements, the policy stops changing. That's the optimal policy. Look at the shape: a staircase. The more cars piled up at the first place, the more you move. And the value: from about four hundred twenty dollars with an empty lot, to about six hundred forty with twenty cars at each. Why push cars to the second place? More customers there, and fewer returns. It keeps running dry. And never move more than you need. Every car costs two dollars, and a car in the wrong place earns nothing. None of this was programmed in. It fell out of evaluate and improve.

13.title: How much evaluation?
13.text: Look how long each evaluation took: a hundred twenty-six sweeps, then ninety-one, eighty, forty-five, fourteen. Each new policy starts from the old values, so evaluation gets faster as we go. Do we really need to evaluate all the way? Or can we stop when we're close? Stop early, and each step is cheaper. But the promise that each step improves gets weaker. Truncated evaluation. Cost-wise, one sweep is about m times n squared operations, with m actions and n states. Much less than n cubed, since we usually have far fewer actions than states. In practice, people stop early all the time. And it works. Push it to the extreme: one sweep, then improve. That has a name, and it's next episode.

13.title: An iteration of two problems
13.text: So here's the big picture. In supervised learning, you have one problem: fit the data. Reinforcement learning isn't one problem. It's an iteration of two: evaluation and control. Evaluate, to know where you stand. Then improve, to move. And repeat. You'll see these two steps inside almost every algorithm from now on. Sometimes in disguise. Next time: value iteration, and how to sweep smarter. With me so far?

14.title: Back up the max
14.text: Last time: evaluate a policy all the way, then improve it. What if we evaluate for just one sweep? Take the Bellman optimality equation, the one with the max, and turn it into an update. Policy iteration evaluates all the way, then improves. Value iteration improves after every single sweep. Value at k plus one: the max over actions of the reward, plus γ times the value at k of where you land. That's value iteration. Improvement and evaluation, squeezed into one line. Why does it work? If the values stop changing, they satisfy the Bellman optimality equation. And the only thing that does is v star. And each round is cheap: one sweep, no full evaluation inside.

14.title: The shortest path
14.text: Watch it on a tiny maze. A four by four grid, the goal in the top-left corner, minus one for every step. Sweep one: the goal is zero, everything else minus one. Sweep two: the goal's neighbours stay at minus one. Everyone else drops to minus two. Sweep three: minus three appears. The ripple grows by one ring per sweep. Each sweep, the news travels one step further from the goal. Like a ripple in a pond. By sweep six, every square knows its distance to the goal. One more sweep changes nothing. And notice: no explicit policy in between. The middle values might not belong to any policy at all. Only the final ones matter. And the policy at the end? In every square, step to the neighbour with the highest value. Greedy on v star. On this maze, value iteration does what a breadth-first search would do. But it works on any MDP, with randomness and rewards anywhere.

14.title: Three algorithms
14.text: So now we have three dynamic-programming algorithms. Let's put them in one table. Prediction, with the Bellman expectation equation: iterative policy evaluation. Control, with the expectation equation plus greedy improvement: policy iteration. Control, with the optimality equation: value iteration. All three need the model, and all three update every state, every sweep. That's called synchronous. Cost per sweep: m times n squared for state values. For action values, m squared times n squared. One reason we usually prefer v when we have the model. So the whole table is two questions: prediction or control, and which Bellman equation you turn into an update.

14.title: Asynchronous, in place
14.text: But who says you have to update every state, every time, in order? Asynchronous dynamic programming: update states one at a time, in any order. As long as every state keeps getting picked, it still converges. Picture a hundred workers, each updating their own corner of the map, whenever they're ready. Three simple ideas. First: in-place. Keep one copy of the values, not two. As soon as a state gets a new value, the next state uses it. News spreads faster, and you save memory. And the order matters. Sweep from the goal outwards, and one sweep can do the work of many. Synchronous is the textbook. Asynchronous is what people actually code.

14.title: Prioritised sweeping
14.text: Second: prioritised sweeping. Some states are badly wrong. Others are already right. Measure how wrong each one is: the gap between its value and what Bellman says it should be. Update the most wrong first. Then fix its neighbours, because their gaps just changed. Like a priority queue in an emergency room. In big problems, most states are fine most of the time. Prioritising saves a lot of work. Same instinct as a good doctor. Worst cases first. Don't spend time on the healthy

14.title: Real-time DP
14.text: ones. Third: real-time dynamic programming. Only update the states the agent actually visits, or expects to visit soon. A chess player doesn't think about impossible positions. Why should Bit? In a maze, Bit doesn't need perfect values in rooms he'll never enter. Spend your computation where the action is. That's how planning in games works: think hard about the positions you might actually reach, and ignore the rest of the universe.

14.title: Sample backups
14.text: One more problem. Every backup we did was full-width. To update one state, you look at every action, and every possible next state. Fine for a grid. For a big problem, even one backup is too expensive. That's the curse of dimensionality. And it needs p. All of it. Perfectly. The fix: sample backups. Instead of all the next states, use one that actually happened: a state, an action, a reward, a next state. And then you don't need p at all. The world does the sampling for you. That's model-free learning, and it's coming soon. Keep this sentence in mind: model-free learning is dynamic programming with samples instead of expectations.

14.title: Module three, done
14.text: And that's module three, done. We have Markov decision processes, returns, values, and the Bellman equations. And three ways to solve them when we know the model: evaluation, policy iteration, value iteration. All of it rests on one equation, from one man, in the nineteen fifties. But why does any of this converge? Why one answer, and why from any starting point? Next module: the theory. Contractions, fixed points, and one beautiful theorem. With me so far? See you there.

15.title: The map on the floor
15.text: Here's a trick. Take a map of this room, and drop it on the floor of this room. Somewhere on that map, there's exactly one point lying right on top of the spot it shows. Exactly one. Always. Wherever the map lands, however it's turned. As long as the whole map lies inside the room. Rotated, crumpled a bit, it doesn't matter. Today's question is why value iteration and policy evaluation always converge. And it's the same reason that map works.

15.title: The worst state
15.text: First, we need a way to say how far apart two value functions are. Take two guesses for the values, u and v. Compare them state by state, and keep the biggest gap. That's the max norm. The distance between two value functions is the worst state. Two guesses that agree everywhere, except one state where they differ by ten? The distance is ten. Not the average state. The worst. Bit is only as right as his most wrong state. Why not the average? Because a disaster in one state can hide behind a good average.

15.title: Contractions
15.text: Now, an operator: a machine that takes a whole value function in, and gives a whole value function out. It's a contraction if it pulls any two inputs closer together, by a fixed factor smaller than one. Distance before: d. Distance after: at most α times d, with α below one. And a fixed point is an input that comes out unchanged. T of x equals x. Like a thermostat set to twenty-one degrees. It pushes the room there, and once it's there, it stays. The map on the floor is a contraction of the room. And the point that lies on its own spot? The fixed point.

15.title: Banach's theorem
15.text: Now the beautiful theorem, from Stefan Banach, nineteen twenty-two. If T is a contraction on a complete space, then first: it has exactly one fixed point. Not two. Not zero. One. Second: start anywhere, apply T, apply it again, and again. You always land on that point. And third, it's fast: after n steps, the error is at most α to the n, times the error you started with. Geometric convergence. Every step chops off the same fraction of what's left. Banach proved this in his doctoral thesis. Not bad, for a thesis.

15.title: The Bellman operator
15.text: Now look at value iteration again. One sweep takes a value function, and returns a new one. For every state: the max over actions, of the reward plus γ times the expected value of where you land. Call that machine T star, the Bellman optimality operator. Value iteration is just: apply T star, again and again. Picture it: every possible value function is a point in a huge space. T star moves points around in that space. And T star is a contraction, with factor γ. So Banach does the rest.

15.title: The proof in one picture
15.text: Why is it a contraction? One picture. Take two guesses, u and v, that differ by at most d, anywhere. Average them over the next states: the averages differ by at most d. Averaging never stretches a gap. Multiply by γ: now at most γ times d. Add the same reward to both: the gap doesn't change. And taking the max over actions can't stretch it either. So every sweep shrinks the worst gap by at least γ. That's the whole proof. No calculus. Just three facts. Averages don't stretch gaps. Maxes don't stretch gaps. And γ shrinks them. Three facts come out: there's one fixed point, v star. Value iteration reaches it from any start. And T star is monotone: bigger input, bigger output. Monotone matters too. Start below v star, and you stay below it, creeping up on every sweep.

15.title: Our numbers
15.text: We tried it on a small random MDP we made up: ten states, two actions, γ at point nine. The error starts at about four point six. After forty sweeps: about point zero six. That's about seventy-five times smaller. And the bound, γ to the k, sits right on top of it the whole way. With γ at point nine, every twenty-two sweeps cut the error at least ten times. With γ at point nine nine, you need about two hundred thirty sweeps for the same cut. Looking far ahead costs computation.

15.title: One idea behind DP
15.text: Same story for policy evaluation. Drop the max, average over what π picks instead. Call it T π. Also a γ-contraction. Also monotone. Its one fixed point is v π. So iterative policy evaluation converges too, from any starting guess. And the same holds for q functions. So every algorithm from module three is secretly the same thing: apply a contraction until it stops moving. This is why I keep saying this course makes good promises. Here's the proof. Value iteration: apply T star. Policy evaluation: apply T π. Policy iteration: alternate evaluating with T π and improving greedily. But all of this assumed we know p and can store every value exactly. Next time: what breaks when we can't. With me so far?

16.title: Two luxuries
16.text: Everything so far assumed two luxuries. We know the MDP perfectly, and we can store every value exactly. In real life? We usually get neither. We don't know p, so we estimate the Bellman update from samples. That adds sampling error. And we can't keep a table with a value for every chess board. So we fit a function: a linear model, or a neural network. That adds approximation error. Two errors, from two directions. Sometimes they cancel. Usually, they don't. The goal stays the same: a policy that's optimal, or at least close. This is where deep RL lives: big networks, and samples instead of the true model.

16.title: Approximate value iteration
16.text: Approximate value iteration: apply T star, then squeeze the result back into our function class. For example, choose the parameters that minimise the squared distance to the Bellman target, over the states. It sounds harmless. Fit a little, update a little, repeat. Does it still converge to v star? In general… no. The fitting step isn't a contraction in the max norm. Banach's promise is gone. Each fit on its own is fine. It's the repetition that hurts.

16.title: A divergence example
16.text: Here's a famous example, from Tsitsiklis and Van Roy. Two states, one parameter, θ. The first state's value is θ. The second's is two θ. All rewards are zero, and there are no decisions. The first state always moves to the second. The second stays put, except with a small chance, ε, the episode ends. All rewards are zero, so the true values are zero. Easy, right? Fit θ by least squares to the targets. Work through the algebra, and each step multiplies θ by six minus four ε, times γ, over five. With ε one eighth and γ equal to one, that's one point one. Start at one. Ten steps: two point six. Thirty steps: seventeen. The truth is zero, and the estimate runs away. Why? The fit cares about both states at once. To fix the second state, it pushes θ up, and drags the first state with it. Notice: with γ at point nine, the factor is point nine nine, and it slowly converges. Divergence needs γ above about point nine one. So the danger is real. But it needs the right conditions. Or the wrong ones.

16.title: Hopeless? Not quite
16.text: Hopeless? Not quite. Sampled, online versions of these algorithms do converge, under mild conditions. Even with function approximation, the danger of divergence rarely shows up in practice. And in this very example, there's a fix: weight each state by how often you actually visit it. Then it converges. And remember: we don't need the values to be right. We need them to be in the right order. Many value functions give the same optimal policy.

16.title: How good is a greedy policy?
16.text: Which raises the real question. If my values are a bit wrong, and I act greedily on them, how bad is my policy? There's a theorem for that. Take any q, and its greedy policy π. How much worse π is than optimal, is at most two γ over one minus γ, times how far q is from q star. Read it as an exchange rate. Value error goes in, performance loss comes out. Small errors in values, small loss in performance. Graceful. If your q is off by at most some small amount everywhere, your greedy policy loses at most that factor times that amount.

16.title: Reading the factor
16.text: Let's read the factor. γ at point nine: eighteen. γ at point nine nine: about two hundred. So the longer you look ahead, the more a small value error can cost you. Errors compound along the way. So with long horizons, invest in accurate values. They're worth it. γ equals zero: the factor is zero. Why? With no future, every policy has the same q: just the immediate reward. Nothing to get wrong. And if q equals q star, the bound is zero: being greedy on q star is optimal. Matches what we said in module three.

16.title: The proof
16.text: The proof is five lines. Add and subtract T π of q, then use the triangle inequality. Because π is greedy on q, T π of q equals T star of q. Then use the contraction, twice. Collect the terms, and divide by one minus γ. That's where the factor comes from. Not deep. Just the same contraction trick, used twice.

16.title: Module four, done
16.text: And approximate policy iteration? Evaluate approximately, improve greedily. Do the values converge to q star? In general, no. Does the policy converge to the optimal one? In general, also no. It depends on the approximation. We'll come back to that when we meet function approximation properly. Deep RL papers spend a lot of effort fighting exactly this instability. So, module four. Exact dynamic programming converges, because Bellman operators are contractions. Approximate dynamic programming can break that promise. But greedy policies degrade gracefully, and we know by how much. Being greedy is safe, as long as your values are good. Next module: we drop the model completely, and learn from experience. With me so far? See you in module five.

17.title: No model
17.text: For two whole modules, Bit knew the rules of the world: p, every probability, every reward. Today we take that away. No model. Bit doesn't know how the world works. He only gets to play. There's a theorem: sample the world forever, and you'll know it exactly. Very nice. Good luck sampling even a small game perfectly. So we need methods that learn well from a finite pile of experience. First goal: prediction. Given a policy, learn its values, from samples only. Two methods, this episode and the next: Monte Carlo, and temporal differences. Today, Monte Carlo.

17.title: Monte Carlo
17.text: Method one is named after a casino: Monte Carlo. The idea is almost embarrassingly simple. Play. See what happened. Average. The name? The casino in Monaco. Rolling dice, many, many times. That's the whole method. You already did this, in module two. A bandit: for each handle, average the rewards you got. That's Monte Carlo. Now add states. Each state is its own little bandit. The episodes still last one step, and actions don't change the next state. Like showing an ad to a user: the user is the state, the ad is the action, a click is the reward. Average the clicks for each kind of user and each ad, and you have a value for every pair.

17.title: Features
17.text: But with millions of users, you can't keep a table with one number per user. So describe each state with a few features: numbers like age, time of day, past clicks. Call that vector x of s. And make the value a weighted sum of the features: v of s is w times x of s. A linear value function. And here's a nice surprise: a table is a special case. Give each state its own feature, one for that state, zero for everything else. One-hot features, and the weights are exactly the table entries. A linear model sounds weak. With good features, it goes surprisingly far.

17.title: Learning the weights
17.text: How do we learn w? Minimise the squared error between what happened and what we predicted. Take a gradient step: move w by α, times the error, times the features. Error times feature. Features that were on get the blame, or the credit. Same idea as supervised learning, with the return as the label. And with one-hot features, this is exactly the incremental average from module two. Same formula, new clothes.

17.title: Whole episodes
17.text: Now, real sequences. Bit plays a whole episode with his policy: state, action, reward, state, and so on, until it ends. For every state he visited, compute the return from there: everything that came after. Then nudge that state's value toward the return. Or just average all the returns you ever saw from it. Count a state once per episode, or every time it appears. First visit, or every visit. Both converge. And the step size: one over the number of visits gives the exact average. A constant α slowly forgets old games, which helps if the world changes. By the law of large numbers, from module two, the average converges to the true value. No p anywhere.

17.title: Blackjack
17.text: Let's try it on Blackjack. This is the example we played with in class. It's a nice fit: every game is an episode, it always ends, and the rules are a pain to write down as probabilities. You want your cards to sum closer to twenty-one than the dealer's, without going over. The state: your sum, from twelve to twenty-one. The dealer's visible card, ace to ten. And whether you hold a usable ace. Ten times ten times two: two hundred states. Below twelve, you always take a card; you can't go bust. Three numbers describe the whole situation. Near enough, that's the Markov state of Blackjack. Actions: stick, or take another card. The reward comes only at the end: plus one for a win, zero for a draw, minus one for a loss. The policy we'll evaluate: stick on twenty or twenty-one, otherwise always take a card. Bold. Maybe too bold.

17.title: What it learned
17.text: We ran it. After ten thousand games, the values are bumpy. Especially with a usable ace: those states are rare, so there's little data. After half a million games, the surface is smooth. Half a million games, in seconds, on a laptop. Try that at a real casino. And look: it's only high at twenty and twenty-one. Everywhere else, this policy loses money. Hitting on nineteen is not a great plan. And when the dealer shows an ace, everything drops. Monte Carlo found all of that without knowing a single rule of the game. Two hundred states, and ten thousand games still leave holes. Now imagine chess.

17.title: The catch
17.text: So what's the catch? Monte Carlo has to wait until the episode ends. Only then is the return known. Long episodes: slow learning. Episodes that never end: no learning at all. And because each return adds up many random steps, it's noisy. Can we learn before we know how the story ends? Yes. Next time: temporal differences. With me so far?

18.title: Sample the Bellman equation
18.text: Remember the Bellman equation: the value of a state is the expected reward, plus γ times the value of the next state. Dynamic programming computes that expectation, using p. Temporal-difference learning says: I don't have p. But I just took one step. Let me use that one step as a sample. That's the whole idea. The rest is details. It's Bellman's equation again, with one sample instead of the full average.

18.title: The TD update
18.text: So: Bit is in a state. He acts, gets a reward, and lands in the next state. His target: the reward, plus γ times his current guess for the next state. Nudge the old value toward that target, by a step size α. The gap between the target and the old value has a name: the TD error, δ. In Monte Carlo, we had the return in our hands. In TD, we don't. We hold the reward we just got, plus our previous best guess. That's TD's return. If the next state turned out better than expected, δ is positive, and the value goes up. Worse than expected, it goes down. And notice: no p anywhere. The world just handed Bit the next state. Learning a guess from a guess. It sounds like cheating. It works. The reward is real. Only the rest is a guess. Each step, a little more truth gets in.

18.title: Online, and the square
18.text: And it's online. You act, and you learn. Right away, after every step. Monte Carlo waits for the end of the episode. Like tasting the soup every minute while you cook, instead of waiting until the guests have left. Now, my favourite figure: the square. Every method lives in a two-dimensional space. How deep you look down the tree, and how wide. One step, one branch: that's TD. The whole branch, to the end: Monte Carlo. One step, but every child: dynamic programming. And the whole tree, everything: exhaustive search. TD and dynamic programming both look one step ahead. The difference: DP averages over every next state. TD uses the one that actually happened. So in the square, TD is the cheap corner. One step, one sample. Four corners, four algorithms. Everything else lives somewhere in between.

18.title: Bootstrapping and sampling
18.text: Two words to keep them apart. Bootstrapping: the update uses an estimate. Dynamic programming and TD bootstrap. Monte Carlo doesn't. Sampling: the update uses one sample instead of an expectation. Monte Carlo and TD sample. Dynamic programming doesn't. TD is the one that does both: it samples, and it bootstraps. And the same trick works for action values. TD on q has its own name, SARSA. We'll meet it next module.

18.title: A trick question
18.text: A trick question. Is a dynamic-programming update bigger than a TD update? Than a Monte Carlo one? Bigger than TD: TD looks at one action, DP at all of them. Than Monte Carlo? It depends. Ten children below you, but a branch a hundred steps long? Monte Carlo looks at more. So the size of an update isn't about the method's name. It's about the shape of the tree. Good exam question, by the way. You didn't hear it from me.

18.title: Driving home
18.text: A classic example: driving home. Leaving the office, I predict thirty minutes. Reaching the car, it's raining: forty in total. The highway goes well: thirty-five. Then I get stuck behind a truck: forty again. Entering my street: forty-three. And I arrive after forty-three minutes. Elapsed time, plus predicted time to go: that's the predicted total. Watch it move. Monte Carlo waits until I'm home, then pulls every prediction toward forty-three. TD adjusts each prediction toward the next one, as I drive. Stuck behind the truck? I already know I was too optimistic on the highway. By the time I'm home, TD has already done most of the learning.

18.title: Bias and variance
18.text: So TD can learn before knowing the final outcome. From incomplete episodes. Even in tasks that never end. A robot that runs for weeks never reaches an end. TD learns anyway. There's a price, though. The Monte Carlo return is an unbiased estimate of the value. It's what really happened. The TD target uses a guess, so it's biased. Until the guesses are right. But the Monte Carlo return depends on many random actions, rewards and transitions. Lots of noise. The TD target depends on only one step. Monte Carlo: no bias, high variance. TD: some bias, low variance. The classic trade-off. Lower variance means smoother learning: fewer wild jumps, and usually a bigger step size you can afford. In practice, TD often learns faster.
