But Monte Carlo is more robust when the state isn't really Markov. More on that next time.

18.title: Do they agree?
18.text: So which one wins? Same data, same world: do they even agree? With enough data and a step size that shrinks properly, both converge to the true values. The question is what happens before that. Spoiler: on finite data, they can disagree. And both are right. Next time: random walks, and a case where they give different answers. Both, kind of, right. With me so far?

19.title: A random walk
19.text: Last time: Monte Carlo and TD, two ways to learn values from experience. Today, let's race them. The track: a random walk. Five squares in a row, A to E. Bit starts in the middle, on C. Each step, he moves left or right, fifty-fifty. Fall off the right end: one point. Fall off the left: nothing. So the only reward in the whole world sits at the far right edge. So a square's value is the chance of finishing on the right. From the middle: one half. The true values are easy to work out. A is worth one sixth. Each square to the right adds one more sixth, up to five sixths for E. Why such a toy? Because we know the right answer, so we can measure the error exactly.

19.title: TD learns it
19.text: Start every guess at one half, and run TD with a step size of point one. After the first episode, only one value moved. Bit fell off the left end, and only A felt it. Every other step compared one half with one half. No surprise, no update. After ten episodes, a slope appears. After a hundred, it's close to the truth. Notice the edges learn first. That's where things actually happen. E sits next to the reward, so it learns fast. A sits next to nothing, so it learns from its neighbour. Information flows backwards, one step at a time, from where the rewards are. With a step size of point one, the guesses never fully settle. They jiggle around the truth. A smaller step: smoother, but slower.

19.title: The race
19.text: Now the race. A hundred runs, a hundred episodes each, and we measure the average error. Monte Carlo, with a few step sizes. Then TD. On this problem, TD learns faster, for every step size we tried. And look at the TD curves. The biggest step size is fastest at first, then stalls higher. The smallest is slow, but ends lowest. Not a theorem, by the way. But a pattern you'll see a lot. Monte Carlo pays for its noise. Every return depends on the whole random path. TD pays for its bias. Early on, it leans on guesses that are still wrong.

19.title: Batch learning
19.text: Now a different question. Suppose the data is fixed. Just a handful of episodes, and no more. Replay them again and again, until the values stop moving. That's called batch learning. That's the situation in many real projects: you have a log of data, and that's all you'll get. A log of driving data, a hospital's records, a history of games. Fixed. Squeeze everything out of it. With infinite data, both methods find the true values. With finite data, do they agree?

19.title: A and B
19.text: Two states, A and B. No discounting. Eight episodes. Once: A, reward zero, then B, reward zero, the end. Six times: B, reward one, the end. And once: B, reward zero, the end. What's the value of B? Six good endings out of eight: three quarters. Everyone agrees. What's the value of A? Think about it for a second. Pause the video if you like. I'll wait. Who would you bet on? Monte Carlo says zero. The only time we saw A, the return was zero. TD says three quarters. A always went to B, with reward zero, and B is worth three quarters. Same data. Two answers. Zero, and three quarters.

19.title: Who's right?
19.text: So who's right? Both. They're answering different questions. Monte Carlo finds the values that best fit the returns it actually saw. Minimum squared error. TD finds the values of the most likely Markov model behind the data. In that model, A always leads to B. And B pays one, three times out of four. TD assumes the world is Markov: what happens after B doesn't care how you got there. It builds the model in its head, without ever writing it down, and answers as if that model were true. It's called the certainty-equivalence estimate: assume your estimated model is the truth, and solve it. With more and more data, both would agree. It's only the finite data that splits them.

19.title: The Markov difference
19.text: That's the deep difference. TD exploits the Markov property. Monte Carlo doesn't. When the world is Markov, that's a big advantage: TD squeezes more out of the same data. When it isn't? Say Bit only sees part of the state. Then Monte Carlo is safer: it never assumes anything about what comes next. And partial observability is everywhere in robotics. A camera only sees what's in front of it. Remember module one: is the weather Markov? Not really. Then trust the returns. In practice, people mix the two. That's exactly where we go next.

19.title: Which to trust
19.text: So: TD usually learns faster, and uses the Markov structure. Monte Carlo makes fewer assumptions. Neither is always better. Know what each one assumes. One looks one step ahead. The other looks all the way to the end. Trust your state? TD. Don't trust it? Monte Carlo. Do we have to choose? What about looking three steps ahead? Or ten? Next time. With me so far?

20.title: Two extremes
20.text: TD looks one step ahead, and leans on a guess. If the guess is bad, the update is biased. And news travels back slowly, one step per episode. Monte Carlo looks all the way to the end. News travels fast, but the updates are noisy. Each has exactly the strength the other one lacks. TD trusts its guesses too early. Monte Carlo trusts nothing but the end. So why not something in between?

20.title: n-step returns
20.text: The n-step return: add up the next n real rewards, then lean on the guess n steps ahead. n equals one: that's TD. n equals two: two rewards, then a guess. And n equals infinity, all the way to the end: Monte Carlo. Two steps, written out: the next reward, plus γ times the one after, plus γ squared times the guess two steps ahead. It's a dial. TD on one end, Monte Carlo on the other. Same update rule as before. Only the target changes.

20.title: Which n?
20.text: Does the middle help? We tried it on a longer random walk: nineteen squares. Minus one on the left, plus one on the right. Ten episodes, a hundred runs, every step size from zero to one, and n from one up to five hundred twelve. The winner: n equals four. Not one, not infinity. Somewhere in the middle. That's our own run, by the way. A hundred runs per setting, ten episodes each. And a large n with a large step size? Worse than not learning at all. Too much noise. Why the middle? Short steps lean on bad early guesses. Long ones drown in noise. On another problem, the best n will be different.

20.title: The λ-return
20.text: But which n? Why choose at all? Mix them. The λ-return: a weighted average of all the n-step returns. One step gets weight one minus λ. Two steps get a bit less. Each further step, multiply by λ again. λ equals zero: only one step. That's TD. λ equals one: everything goes to the end. That's Monte Carlo. And the weights add up to one. A proper average. Same trick as γ: one over one minus λ is roughly the horizon. λ at point nine is like looking about ten steps ahead. So λ is a dial too, but a smooth one. No need to pick a whole number of steps.

20.title: The forward view
20.text: There's a catch. To compute the λ-return, you need the whole future. You're back to waiting for the end, like Monte Carlo. And for tasks that never end, there is no end to wait for. That's the forward view: stand in a state, and look ahead. Now flip it. Stand in the present, and look back. Instead of asking what comes next, each new error asks: who deserves the credit?

20.title: Eligibility traces
20.text: Every state Bit visits leaves a trace behind, like a footprint in wet sand. Visit a state: its trace jumps up. Then, every step, all traces fade, by γ times λ. Visit a state twice in a row, and its trace stacks up. Leave it alone, and it fades. With λ at zero, traces vanish at once: plain TD. With λ at one, they fade only by γ. When something surprising happens, a TD error, it's sent backwards to every state, in proportion to its trace. Recent states get more credit. Frequent states get more credit. That's an eligibility trace. Each state keeps its own trace. With features, it's one trace per weight.

20.title: Beep, beep, beep, flash
20.text: A little story. Bit hears a beep, a beep, a beep, then sees a flash, and gets a star. What earned the star? Recency says: the flash, it came last. Frequency says: the beep, it happened three times. The trace blends both. The beep's footprint built up, three times. The flash's is fresh. The trace doesn't decide who's right. It spreads the credit, and many episodes sort it out. Animal psychologists asked this exact question long before computers did.

20.title: Monte Carlo = sum of TD errors
20.text: And here's the beautiful part. If the values stay fixed during an episode, the Monte Carlo error is exactly the sum of the discounted TD errors. So with λ equal to one, traces add up to the Monte Carlo update. But they do it one step at a time, as you go. No waiting. No storing the future. Constant work per step, whatever the horizon. That's why traces are everywhere: they turn a look-ahead method into a look-back one. And with λ in between, you get the λ-return's update, approximately, online. The backward view gives you the forward view's answer, without the waiting.

20.title: Module five, done
20.text: And that's module five, done. Without a model, Bit can now predict: Monte Carlo, TD, n-step returns, and λ with traces. He can tell how good a policy is. But he still can't find a better one. And the same ideas come right back for control, with q instead of v. Five modules in. The next one is where Bit finally learns to act. Next module: control without a model. Q-learning, SARSA, and a trip to the casino. With me so far? See you there.

21.title: From predicting to acting
21.text: Five modules in, Bit can predict. Give him a policy, and he'll tell you how good it is. But nobody wants a critic. We want Bit to act, and to get better at it. Today he learns to act. No model, no map. Just experience. Remember the recipe from dynamic programming? Evaluate the policy. Improve it. Repeat. That loop is called generalised policy iteration. Today we run it without a model.

21.title: Why q, not v
21.text: Here's the snag. To improve greedily with v, you need to know where each action leads. Which states come next, and how likely each one is. That's a model, and we don't have one. So learn q instead. q of s and a: how good is this action, right here. With q, improving is easy. Look at the row for your state, and take the biggest number. Like choosing a dish from reviews. You don't need to know what happens in the kitchen. Monte Carlo and TD can learn q from experience. Same methods as before, one letter different. So for control, we learn q, not v. That's the whole trick of this module.

21.title: Greedy is a trap
21.text: But pure greedy is a trap. Say the first action you tried paid off a little. Greedy will pick it forever. The other actions never get a chance to show what they're worth. So we explore. ε-greedy: most of the time, take the best action. Once in a while, a random one. And the theory backs it up. An ε-greedy policy built on your q is never worse than the policy you had. Small detail: the random move can land on the best action too. Exploring includes the obvious.

21.title: The cleaning robot
21.text: Now, how big should ε be? In class, I used a cleaning robot. Fix ε at point one, and ten percent of the time it does random things in your living room. That's not why you bought it. You want ε to shrink. One over k works well, where k counts the episodes. Day one, it explores a lot. By the two hundredth run, it should know the house. And one over k never quite reaches zero. A sliver of curiosity stays, and keeps shrinking. Nobody wants a robot that's still curious about the couch after a year.

21.title: GLIE
21.text: That gives us a condition with a funny name: GLIE. Greedy in the limit, with infinite exploration. Two promises. Every state and action gets tried infinitely often. And in the end, the policy becomes greedy. Keep both, and Monte Carlo control finds the optimal action values. A strong guarantee. But notice the second half. I do ask you to stop exploring eventually. At the optimum, every random move is a wrong move.

21.title: SARSA
21.text: Monte Carlo waits for the end of an episode. We already know the fix: TD. TD on q has a name you can pronounce: SARSA. The name is the data it needs: a state and an action, the reward, then the next state and the next action. Nudge q of S and A toward the reward, plus γ times q of the next pair. Start the table at zeros. The start state is given, like in chess, or random, like the cards you're dealt. Then act ε-greedily on q, and update after every single step. Update the policy after every step, or after every few episodes? Every step is smoother, but noisier. Which is better? There's no way to know in advance. Solve that in general, and that's great. If not, I won't be mad.

21.title: Step sizes that behave
21.text: Does SARSA find the optimum? Yes, with GLIE, and with step sizes that behave. Two conditions on the step sizes. Their sum must be infinite. The sum of their squares must be finite. α equal to one over t passes both. The harmonic series grows forever. After a million steps it's only about fourteen point four, but it never stops. The squares add up to π squared over six. About one point six four. Big enough to get anywhere. Small enough to settle

21.title: Ten lines and a windy gridworld
21.text: down. All those slides of maths. And in code, it's about ten lines of Python. Borderline funny how simple it is. That's how good ideas usually look. We ran it on a windy gridworld. In the middle columns, the wind pushes Bit upwards. The first episode takes about seven hundred steps. Bit gets blown around a lot. After a hundred and seventy episodes, about eight thousand steps in all, an episode takes about twenty two steps. The shortest possible path is fifteen. Our own runs: fifty of them, ε at point one, step size one half. The curve gets steeper as Bit learns. Why not fifteen? Because ε still throws in a random move now and then, and the wind punishes every one.

21.title: On-policy
21.text: SARSA is on-policy. It learns the value of the policy it actually follows, random moves included. That sounds like a detail. It isn't. It changes which path Bit thinks is best. Learn q, explore, shrink the exploration slowly, and update with SARSA. That's model-free control. Next time: learning about one policy while following another. Q-learning, and a walk along a cliff.

22.title: Behaviour vs target
22.text: SARSA learns about the policy it follows. Today, Bit learns about one policy while following another. The one you follow is the behaviour policy. Call it μ. The one you want to learn about is the target policy, π. When they're the same, that's on-policy. When they differ, off-policy. Why would anyone want that? In class, I gave three reasons. SARSA can't do that. It learns about whatever it does, mistakes included.

22.title: Why off-policy?
22.text: One. A robot vacuum explores the house with a random walk. But what you want to know is the best route. Two. You want to become a good chess player. But all you do is solve two-move chess puzzles. Three. Learn from someone else: another agent, a human, an oracle. Their experience, your policy. In all three, the behaviour gathers the data, and the target is what we actually want. And one pile of exploration can serve many goals. The same walk teaches the way to the kitchen, and to the living room. The price: when μ and π are very different, learning is slower. Off-policy learning lets one stream of experience teach many lessons.

22.title: Q-learning
22.text: The most famous off-policy method is Q-learning. SARSA uses the next action Bit actually takes. Q-learning uses the best next action: the max. So the target is greedy, whatever Bit really does next. Exploration doesn't leak into the values. Written out: q of S and A moves toward the reward, plus γ times the biggest q in the next state. It converges to the optimal q, as long as every pair keeps getting visited and the step sizes behave. The behaviour can be anything that keeps exploring. ε-greedy is the usual choice. One word changed. Next action became best action. Let's see what that does.

22.title: The cliff
22.text: A grid, four rows by twelve. Start bottom left, goal bottom right. Between them, along the bottom edge, a cliff. Step off, and you lose a hundred and go back to the start. Every other step costs one. So the shortest path, hugging the edge, scores minus thirteen. A hundred points of penalty for a single slip. That's a steep price. Both learners explore with ε at point one. One random move in ten. Bit doesn't know any of this. He just walks, falls, and learns. Watch the two paths closely. This is where the two methods part ways.

22.title: Our run
22.text: Our own run: five hundred episodes, a hundred runs each. Q-learning finds the edge path. Thirteen steps. Optimal. SARSA picks a path away from the edge. Longer, but safe. Now look at the reward while they learn. SARSA earns about minus twenty six per episode. Q-learning earns about minus fifty. Walking the edge, with one random step in ten, it falls about once every three episodes. That's a hundred runs averaged, so the gap is real, not luck. Q-learning learned the better policy. SARSA earns more while exploring. Why the gap? Q-learning's values assume a perfect, greedy walker. But the real walker still makes random moves, right next to the edge. SARSA's values include its own random moves. So it learns that the edge is dangerous, for someone like itself.

22.title: Which one?
22.text: So which one is better? It depends on whether the falling is real. A real robot next to a real staircase? SARSA's caution is worth a lot. Training in a simulator, then switching exploration off? Q-learning's path is the one you want. And for your own problem, there's no way to know in advance. Many people start with SARSA and switch to Q-learning later. There's no promise that's better either. Methods that choose for you do exist: meta-learning, AutoML. They don't work that well. Yet. Pick one and pray. This course runs on a lot of faith. Faith, and a lot of experiments.

22.title: The flip
22.text: One more thing about Q-learning. It's very loyal to its first guesses. It keeps exploiting whatever looks best, until the estimates of two actions cross. I call that a flip. Starting from scratch, Q-learning is very abusive to its first guesses. It stays put, until a flip. On the reward curve, it looks like noise for a long time. And then, suddenly, a wave. It doesn't converge, doesn't converge, and after three hours it suddenly works. So much fun. Especially when your bonus depends on it.

22.title: How many episodes?
22.text: How many episodes is a lot? Fewer than you think. A hundred thousand episodes is reasonable. For a tiny game, that's a few minutes. Chess, at fifty milliseconds a game: about seventy two thousand games an hour on one core. Four cores: close to three hundred thousand. One hospital resource-allocation project ran fifty million episodes over a weekend. And every one of those episodes is free data. Nobody had to label anything. So don't be shy with episodes. Let it run.

22.title: Recap
22.text: SARSA: on-policy, and careful. Q-learning: off-policy, with a greedy target, and bold. Both are about ten lines of code. Both converge, under the right conditions. And notice: neither one needed a model. Just a table, a step size, and a lot of walking. But Q-learning has a dirty secret. It's too optimistic. Next time, we take it to the casino.

23.title: The max of noisy zeros
23.text: Q-learning takes the max of its estimates. That sounds harmless. It isn't. Take ten actions, all worth exactly zero. Your estimates are noisy: some a bit high, some a bit low. Now pick the biggest. On average, the biggest of ten noisy zeros is about one point five. Ten noisy zeros, and the winner always looks like a genius. Every action is worth zero, and the max says one and a half. That's maximisation bias. The max picks the luckiest error, every single time. And Q-learning doesn't take the max just once. It takes it at every step, and bootstraps on it. The error compounds.

23.title: Two actions
23.text: In class, I told it as a story with two actions. Try each one once. The good action has an unlucky draw. The bad one has a lucky draw. Now Q-learning keeps picking the bad one. The good one barely gets tried, so its low estimate never gets fixed. Until, one day, a flip, and the estimates trade places. The root of it: the same numbers choose the action and score it. That's the trap of using your own estimates for everything. You can't be your own referee.

23.title: The casino
23.text: Now, the casino. Roulette. Bit can bet one dollar on one of a hundred and seventy bets. Or he can stop, and walk away. Every bet loses about five cents on average. Some win big, rarely. Some win small, often. Some bets pay thirty five to one. That's the jackpot Bit remembers. The right answer is to stop. The house always wins. On average. Standard disclaimer: the presenter is not an investment adviser. Q-learning does learn this eventually. It just takes millions of episodes.

23.title: Our roulette run
23.text: We ran our own version: one state, a hundred and seventy bets, γ at point nine five. Q-learning remembers the wins. After a million bets, it thinks a typical bet is worth about a hundred and six dollars. Not minus five cents. Plus a hundred dollars. It would play forever. Every bet looks like a winner, and stopping is worth exactly zero. So it never stops. Double Q-learning, on the very same bets: about minus twenty five cents. A bit gloomy, but it stops betting. Same data. One learner wants to stay all night. The other one goes home.

23.title: Double Q-learning
23.text: So how does double Q-learning work? Keep two tables. One table picks the best action. The other one scores it. Each step, flip a coin and update one of them. To act, use their average. If one table overestimates an action, the other has no reason to agree. So the bias washes out. And acting on their average means you never act on one table's lucky guess alone. The same idea scaled up to Atari games, as double DQN. On a scale where a hundred is a typical human, it improved many games. Atari, by the way, is what we played at the arcade. A big wooden cabinet, a joystick, and another coin every time you lost.

23.title: Importance sampling
23.text: Back to off-policy learning. The data comes from μ, but we want averages under π. A small example. Two actions: left pays one, right pays ten. μ goes left eighty percent of the time. π goes right eighty percent of the time. The plain average of μ's rewards is two point eight. But π's true average is eight point two. The fix: weigh each sample by π over μ. A left counts a quarter. A right counts four times. Now the weighted average is eight point two. A rare action you want more of? Multiply it back up. Formally, you multiply and divide by μ. Multiplying by one never hurt anybody. That's importance sampling. It turns averages under one policy into averages under another. And on average, under μ, the ratio is exactly one. So nothing gets biased.

23.title: Monte Carlo vs TD ratios
23.text: For Monte Carlo, the correction is a product: one ratio for every step of the episode. Ten steps, with a ratio of four each: that's about a million. One unlikely episode gets a weight of a million. The variance explodes. The ratios multiply, so a few rare episodes can dominate everything. TD needs just one ratio, for one step. Much lower variance. That's one reason off-policy methods built on TD are far more common.

23.title: One family
23.text: And for q, there's a cleaner trick. Don't sample the next action at all. Average over all the next actions, weighted by π. That's expected SARSA. If π is greedy, that average is just the max. Expected SARSA becomes Q-learning. Expected SARSA costs a little more per step, but it removes the noise of sampling the next action. So it's really one family. SARSA samples, expected SARSA averages, and Q-learning takes the

23.title: Module six, done
23.text: max. And that's module six, done. Bit can now act without a model. On-policy, off-policy, and without fooling himself. But every method so far keeps a table. One number for every state and action. Three ideas carry over to everything that comes next: exploring, off-policy targets, and double learning. Next module: what to do when the table won't fit. Not in memory. Not in the universe.

24.title: The Q-table
24.text: Module seven. We're past halfway now. So far, every value lived in a table. Rows are states, columns are actions, and each cell holds a q value. The upside: it's child's play. The downsides: it's sparse, because most actions make no sense in most states. It's huge. And it may not fit in memory. And worst of all: the table has no idea that two neighbouring states are related.

24.title: Too many states
24.text: The sentence to remember from this module: too many states to visit them all. Backgammon, a fairly simple game, has about ten to the twenty states. The observable universe has about ten to the eighty atoms. Go has about ten to the hundred and seventy states. Give each state its own atom, and you run out of atoms. And a robot's sensors are continuous: infinitely many states. Chop them into bins, and the count explodes anyway. So we can't visit every state. Not even close. We'll only ever see a sliver of them.

24.title: The gold bag
24.text: Here's the example I use in class. A computer game. You keep finding a bag with ninety nine gold coins. You found it many times, and the reward averaged ninety nine. Now you find a bag with a hundred coins. What's the reward? Everyone says a hundred. Everyone. You just made two hidden assumptions. One: more gold is better. Who told you that? Two: the relation is roughly linear, at least nearby. Ask about a thousand coins, and a room of economists will say less than a thousand. Diminishing returns. Mathematically, it's not true. Practically, it's excellent. Notice what you did: you generalised from states you saw, to a state you never saw.

24.title: Neighbourhoods
24.text: A table can't do that. State ninety nine, visited a hundred times, tells it nothing about state one hundred. They're just two rows. I never defined any relation between them. Functions have neighbourhoods. Anyone remember calculus one? Any calculus one traumas? A neighbourhood is exactly what a table doesn't have. So we write v of s as a function with weights w, and we learn the weights. Nothing changes except the representation. Monte Carlo and TD still work. Pick the weights well, and one learned number covers a whole neighbourhood of states.

24.title: Aggregation and the ladder
24.text: The simplest function is state aggregation. Ninety to a hundred coins? Call it one state. Groups of ten make the problem ten times smaller. But good groups are hard to find in practice. In the gold game, a bag of ninety one and a bag of ninety nine become the same thing. Close enough. Then linear functions: a weight for every feature. Then anything differentiable, like a neural network. Tables and aggregation are special cases of linear. Each step up generalises more, and promises less.

24.title: The rubber band
24.text: And reinforcement learning data is weird. Here's a game from class. Map a room in an hour, by taking random steps. Walk long enough, and you cover every corner. Now play again, tied to one corner with a rubber band. The farther you go, the harder it pulls. We simulated both: twenty thousand steps, in a room of twenty one by twenty one squares. Free, Bit visits every square. Tied, he reaches about a third of the room, and never the far corner. The bias is in the sampling, not in the room. Chess is the same. One game is shaped by its opening. You can't jump to a random board. And Bit chooses his own data. If he exploits, he samples around his current policy, and nowhere else. In supervised learning, someone hands you the data. Here, the learner and the data collector are the same agent. How to sample well, when you're tied to your own experience, is still an open research problem.

24.title: Moving data
24.text: And the data keeps moving. Supervised learning assumes the data doesn't care what you predict. In reinforcement learning, the policy changes as you learn, so the data changes too. Bootstrapping makes the targets move. And sometimes the world itself moves. Warehouse robots in the holiday rush live in a different world than in the quiet season. A student once suggested putting time into the state. Great idea. Doesn't work. So: not independent, and not stationary. Two assumptions of supervised learning, both gone.

24.title: Gradient descent
24.text: So how do we learn the weights? Gradient descent. You know the picture: hills, valleys, and a ball rolling down. Not every course has to reinvent the wheel. The hill is the squared error between the true value and ours. We step downhill, a little at a time. We don't know the true value, so we sample. The update is the step size, times the error, times the gradient. That's stochastic gradient descent. One sample, one small step. And small steps matter. Big ones overshoot the valley. With Monte Carlo, the target is the real return. With TD, it's a reward plus our own guess. Remember that. It'll bite us later.

24.title: Recap
24.text: Too many states, so we generalise. A table remembers. A function guesses, and guessing well is the whole game. Next time: features. Circles, tiles, a car stuck in a valley, and the most dangerous line in statistics.

25.title: Feature vectors
25.text: A linear value function needs features. A feature vector, x of s, describes the state with numbers. The distance of a robot from some landmarks. Trends in the stock market. Which pieces stand where on a chessboard. Then the value is a weighted sum: each feature, times its weight. In the gold game, one feature is enough: the number of coins. Learn a weight of one, and a hundred coins means a hundred. Choose the features, and you choose what the learner can and can't notice.

25.title: The update
25.text: The update is beautifully simple: the step size, times the prediction error, times the feature vector. A classic. Features that were active get the blame, or the credit. The error says how far the prediction missed. The features say which weights were involved. For linear functions, the error surface is a bowl. Monte Carlo slides to the bottom: the best fit there is. You could also log states and returns, and fit a regression afterwards. People do. But the returns are noisy. It converges, but it's noisy. High variance, as always with Monte Carlo.

25.title: Life is not linear
25.text: But life is not linear. Anyone who tells you it's linear is lying. Hooke's law: pull a spring, and the force grows linearly. Up to a point. Pull harder, and the spring deforms, then breaks. Heat it, and the constant changes. Then you meet the second order differential equation, and find out you've been lied to your whole life. So linear only works with good features. And choosing them is the hard part. Physics teachers start with the linear version for a reason. It's a great first approximation. Just not the last one.

25.title: x(s) in code
25.text: A practical note: x of s doesn't really exist in code. There's no function called map to vector. You write the state in your chosen representation from the start. In the gold game, the state already is a number of coins. The feature vector is just that number.

25.title: Coarse coding
25.text: One classic way to build features is coarse coding. Scatter circles over the state space. Each circle is one feature: one if the state is inside it, zero if not. A state lights up a few overlapping circles. Learn from it, and nearby states that share those circles learn too. It's a bit like a mixture of Gaussians, laid over the states. Small circles: narrow, precise generalisation. Big circles: broad and rough, with fewer features to learn. Stretch the circles, and they generalise more in one direction than the other. And the size of the circles is a design choice, made before learning starts.

25.title: Tile coding
25.text: Tile coding is the tidy version. Lay a grid over the space. Then another one, shifted a little. Then another. A state falls into exactly one tile per grid. Eight grids, eight active features. Always. Each grid on its own is coarse. Together, they pin the state down much more finely. And the number of active features never changes, so every update costs the same. Cheap, fast, and surprisingly good. That's why tile coding was a favourite for years, before deep networks took over.

25.title: One point, infinitely many lines
25.text: Now, a warning. Fit a line through one point. How many lines are there? Infinitely many. Your solver hands you one of them: a random line. The most dangerous kind of thing: technically possible, practically terrible. When the variance blows up, the code crashes, and you notice. This one runs fine and returns garbage. And then you debug it forever. With features, the lesson is that each weight needs data from enough different states. A feature that fires in only one state has nothing to generalise from. So when your results look too clean, check how many states each feature has actually seen.

25.title: Mountain Car
25.text: Let's try it on a classic: Mountain Car. A weak car, stuck in a valley. The engine can't climb the hill directly. The car has to rock back and forth to build up speed. The state is position and velocity: two continuous numbers. A table can't hold that. The car starts near the bottom of the valley, with zero speed. Every step costs one, until it reaches the top on the right. Our run: linear SARSA, with eight tilings of eight by eight, averaged over ten runs. All the weights start at zero. Since every step costs one, zero looks optimistic. So the car explores on its own, without ε. The first episode takes about sixteen hundred steps. After three hundred episodes: about a hundred and twenty five. The learned cost to go peaks at the bottom of the valley, standing still. It drops steeply wherever the car already has enough swing. One global line would be terrible here. Many small tiles, each with its own weight, do the job.

25.title: The best you can do
25.text: With function approximation, control reaches the best your approximator can do. A perfect approximator gets you the optimum. Anything less, and it doesn't. That's why, from linear on, I stop promising you the optimum. But the best your approximator can do is often very, very good. And the better the features, the closer that gets to the real thing. Next time: what happens when learning doesn't just miss the optimum, but blows up.

26.title: The ladder of promises
26.text: Every step up the ladder buys power and costs promises. Today, let's be precise about the cost. Tables: a global optimum, guaranteed. The only place in your academic life where anyone ever promised you a global optimum. Linear sits in the middle: reasonable theory, as long as your features are good. Linear: decent answers, especially when states are sampled densely. Any smooth function looks linear up close. Neural networks: the cool kid on the block. Great in practice. No promises at all. Why none? Formally, you could be approximating a function that's continuous everywhere and differentiable nowhere. The Weierstrass function. In class, I first called it Dirichlet. Even the lecturer makes mistakes. So the further up the ladder, the more we lean on practice, and the less on proofs.

26.title: Monte Carlo converges
26.text: Prediction first. Linear Monte Carlo always converges, to the weights with the smallest value error. Unless nothing happens at all. No dynamics, nothing to learn. Monte Carlo sees whole episodes. It has the global picture. Its answer depends only on the data and the features. The state doesn't even have to be Markov. That makes Monte Carlo the safe default, when you can afford to wait.

26.title: TD chases its tail
26.text: TD is different. Its target, a reward plus our own guess, depends on the very weights we're updating. So TD isn't really rolling downhill. It's chasing its own tail. Remember the ball rolling downhill? For TD, the hill moves every time the ball does. Mostly, that's fine. TD belongs to a broader family of stochastic approximation methods, and those usually converge. Usually. Plain gradient descent always converges, with small enough steps and a fixed target. TD's target isn't fixed. When linear TD does converge, it lands near the Monte Carlo answer, not on it. Often faster,

26.title: w and 2w
26.text: though. Here's the classic counterexample. Two states. The first has feature one, the second has feature two. There's one weight, w, so their values are w and two w. The reward between them is zero, so the true values are zero. Now update only the first state, again and again. Its target is γ times two w. If γ is above one half, the target is bigger than w. So w grows. Which makes the target grow. With γ at point nine and a step size of point one, w grows eight percent per update. After a hundred updates, it's twenty two hundred times bigger. The truth is zero. Watch it compound. Every update multiplies w by one point zero eight. After ten updates, w has more than doubled. Nothing in the data is wrong. The rewards are all zero. The explosion comes entirely from the update. And this isn't a rare corner case. Two states, one weight, and it already breaks.

26.title: What saves it
26.text: What saves it? Update both states, on-policy, along the episode. The second state's update pulls w back down, harder. Now w shrinks, by about a third every episode. At γ point nine, that's a multiplier of about point seven per episode. Almost nothing left after twenty episodes. Or use tabular features: one weight per state. Then it's just regression. No explosion. Or look further ahead. With a λ-return, it's safe once λ is above four ninths. Same features, same rewards: converge or explode. It depends on which states you update, and how often.

26.title: The deadly triad
26.text: What went wrong is a combination of three things. Function approximation: states share weights. Bootstrapping: targets use our own guesses. Off-policy: the updates don't follow the episode. Together, they're called the deadly triad. Any two of them are fine. All three, and learning may diverge. Think of a fire triangle: heat, fuel and oxygen. Take one away, and nothing burns. Off-policy shows up even when you don't plan it. Replay old data, and you're off-policy.

26.title: The one table
26.text: If you remember one thing from this module, let it be this table. Monte Carlo converges everywhere: table, linear, nonlinear, on-policy or off. TD on-policy: fine with tables and linear features. Not guaranteed with neural networks. TD off-policy: only the table is safe. For control, the picture is similar. Tabular Q-learning is safe. With function approximation, all bets are off.

26.title: Over the hill
26.text: Why does Monte Carlo do better? Picture a knight galloping up a hill, in thick fog. At the top, is there a higher hill, or a valley? TD is that knight. It only sees one step ahead. Monte Carlo already rode the whole way. It knows what came after the hill. But Monte Carlo needs episodes. If your task never ends, define one anyway: a day, or a week. Or use TD, carefully, and keep an eye on the triad. I once worked on a traffic light project. One junction. An episode was one day. Complaints about that junction: not to me. The day ends, the traffic resets, and you get a return. Imperfect, but usable.

26.title: Tracking
26.text: For control with approximation, the theory is even thinner. And often we don't even want convergence. We want tracking: a policy that keeps adapting as the world changes. That makes sense: the world drifts, and a policy that stopped learning would slowly get worse. Next time: squeeze more out of every sample with batches and replay. And meet DQN.

27.title: Tic-tac-toe
27.text: Let's start with code. In class, we built Q-learning for tic tac toe. Nine squares, so nine actions. Plus one for a win, minus one for a loss, zero for a draw. First question, always: is your reward really what you want? Stop and check. It's usually not trivial. γ is point nine, so Bit looks many moves ahead. And ε is point one. The reward only arrives at the end of the game. Every other move gets zero.

27.title: The weights are the table
27.text: The Q-table starts at zeros. And here's a nice way to see it: the model's weights are the table's values. Look for the policy in the code. There's no policy function anywhere. The policy is implicit. It's the argmax of Q. The update itself is four lines. Elegant to the bone. Short, readable, and it really works. If both players share one table, they play symmetrically. With two tables, they can play differently. And against a random opponent, you learn the best play against a random player. Nothing more.

27.title: Our run
27.text: We ran it: Bit plays crosses against a random opponent, for forty thousand games. After a hundred games, playing greedily, he wins about sixty percent. After forty thousand: about ninety six percent, and he almost never loses. By then, the table holds about two thousand board positions. A nice trick from class: make a video of the table filling in. It looks like abstract art. These are the values of the first move. The centre comes out on top. Another trick: plot the table's average value over time. It's jagged, and more jagged with a bigger ε. Ninety six percent sounds great. But remember who the opponent is. Against a strong opponent, it would have a lot more to learn.

27.title: Least squares TD
27.text: Now, gradient descent uses each experience once, and then throws it away. That's not very sample efficient. Batch methods ask a different question: which weights best fit everything we've seen so far? For linear TD, there's a closed form. Least squares TD: build a matrix and a vector from the data, then solve. Plain TD costs about n operations per step, for n features. Least squares TD costs about n squared. Better answers, more work. It's the same answer TD converges to. You just get it directly, from the data you already have. And you can update it incrementally, one transition at a time, without solving from scratch. Least squares TD extends to q values too, and even to whole policy iteration.

27.title: Experience replay
27.text: Or keep it simple: experience replay. Store the transitions in a buffer. Then sample old ones at random, and update on them again. Each experience gets used many times. And random sampling breaks up the order. One catch: old data came from old policies. Replay is off-policy, whether you like it or not. Replay is also a form of batch learning: go over the past again and again, a little at a time. One more benefit: rare, important experiences don't get lost. They stay in the buffer.

27.title: A network instead
27.text: Now swap the table for a neural network. The observation goes in. One q value per action comes out. Q-learning's update becomes a loss to minimise: the squared TD error. But we stop the gradient through the target. We treat the target as a constant. So it's not a real loss. It just happens to have the right gradient. And we only score the action we took. The other outputs get no feedback on this step. With three actions, the network has three outputs. Each output is one action's q value. The rest is plain deep learning: a mini batch, a gradient step, and an optimiser like

27.title: DQN
27.text: Adam. Put it all together, and you get DQN, from DeepMind, more than ten years ago. A network that maps the screen to action values. ε-greedy exploration. A replay buffer. A second, frozen copy of the network for the targets, refreshed every ten thousand steps or so. And an optimiser. Function approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy replay. All three corners of the deadly triad. And it works. Every piece we met in this module, finally in one place. DQN learned to play dozens of Atari games from the raw pixels, with one recipe. How it gets away with that is the story of the next module.

27.title: Cloud servers
27.text: One more example from class, closer to real work: a cloud of servers. There are small servers and large servers. Jobs come in small, medium and large. The actions: send a job to a small server, send it to a large one, or wait. The reward mixes completion time, utilisation and idle machines. I like giving each part a weight, and playing with the weights. Is that reward correlated with what the client wants? Stop and check. Again. With ε fixed, the reward curve stays noisy. Lower ε slowly, and it settles.

27.title: Module seven, done
27.text: And that's module seven, done. Too many states, so Bit generalises: with features, with tiles, and now with networks. He knows the deadly triad, and the one table to remember. And the code went from a table to a network, without changing the idea. Next module: deep reinforcement learning. Where everything is a vector.

28.title: Minus two
28.text: I didn't remember this lecture's number from the start. But from the end, it was minus two. That's the more important one. Module eight: deep reinforcement learning. A quick recap. All those lovely promises, the global optimum and all. You got so excited. They live over a table. Visit every state and action infinitely many times. Fun in theory. In practice, you won't. Linear functions: decent near the data, bad far from it. Neural networks: great in practice, and in theory we know nothing. Today: why neural networks, how they learn, and what goes in and out.

28.title: Good features?
28.text: The question hanging over this whole course: is our feature vector any good? Good means that states with similar rewards get similar features. But if we knew which states had similar rewards, we wouldn't need to approximate in the first place. So instead of designing the features, let the model learn them. That's what deep learning offers: features learned from data, tuned for your reward.

28.title: Deep is not neural
28.text: First: deep learning is not the same as neural networks. Deep learning means chaining a learning model into itself, again and again. Deep decision trees exist too. Chain trees, and you just get a bigger tree. Not my best example. Draw linear regression as circles and arrows, and you get a perceptron. Stack linear layers, and you still get something linear. You have to break the linearity somewhere. That's the activation function. Don't let anyone tell you stories. Linear is cool, and we add a little non-linear.

28.title: Universal approximation
28.text: And then something remarkable. A big enough network, layer, activation, layer, can approximate any continuous function. We tried it: a bumpy curve, and one hidden layer of tanh units. Two units: a rough sketch. Five units: close. Twenty units: you can barely tell them apart. In theory, any continuous function. In practice, big enough can mean very big. Our own fits, each trained for thirty thousand steps. The error drops about four thousand times, from two units to twenty.

28.title: Two advantages
28.text: As an engineer, I'll tell you: neural networks aren't cheap. They're expensive, hard to train, and hungry for data and memory. Most of the neurons sit idle most of the time. You keep many, and use few. Deep learning has exactly two advantages. Don't let anyone tell you otherwise. One: expressiveness. Two: it learns its own embedding, its own representation. In reinforcement learning, that second one is gold. You don't have to invent a clever state representation.

28.title: Chess, three ways
28.text: Take chess. How do you write down a position? Option one: the board, eight by eight, with a code for each square. Wasteful: most squares are empty. Option two: a list of the pieces, each with its type and its square. Option three: the starting position, plus the list of moves so far. That's what chess notation does. Cheapest, for short games. Which is best? The one that predicts rewards best. And you don't know that in advance. And the best one can change from one task to the next. A deep network says: I don't care about your representation. I'll find a good one for you.

28.title: Everything is a vector
28.text: Which brings me to my favourite claim: everything is a vector. A matrix? Fold it into a vector. A tensor? Fold it twice. A dictionary? Sort it, and line it up. The proof: every data structure sits in memory. And memory is a vector. Even an image: it's just a long row of pixel values. Physics says so. Complaints, please, to the physicists. Not to me. So whatever your state looks like, you can feed it to a network.

28.title: Autodiff
28.text: To train a network, we need gradients. Writing them by hand would be miserable. So we draw the computation as a graph. Inputs flow forward, one operation at a time, to the output. A tiny value network: s times w one, through tanh, times w two, plus a bias. With s equal to two, tanh of one is point seven six, and the value comes out at three point two nine. Now sweep backwards, and multiply the local gradients along the path: three, times point four two, times two. Two point five two. That's the gradient for w one, in a single backward sweep. Where paths merge, you add. That's automatic differentiation. Libraries like JAX do it for you: NumPy, plus gradients, plus a compiler for fast hardware. In code, you write the forward pass. The library writes the backward pass for you.

28.title: What goes in and out
28.text: So what goes in, and what comes out? A value network is just regression: a vector in, one number out. Any regression network works. Put AlexNet in, for laughs. It won't work. Or maybe it will. A policy network: a state in, an action out. Or a state and an action in, and q out. Or a state in, and one output per action. A network with three outputs? Those are three actions' q values. Why not feed in the whole history? It gets huge fast. And the M in MDP stands for Markov: the present state is enough. Our maths works because we don't need the history. The right choice depends on your problem, not on fashion. Next time: why training these networks online is so hard.

29.title: Not i.i.d.
29.text: Supervised deep learning has a quiet assumption: the samples are independent and identically distributed. Shuffle the data, take a mini batch, take a step. Each gradient is an honest sample of the whole picture. Online reinforcement learning breaks that. We update on every new step. And each step grows out of the previous one. The data is strongly correlated. Each new sample looks a lot like the last one. The gradient keeps pointing the same way, for a while. Like learning about a whole city from one street.

29.title: Order matters
29.text: Here's what that does. We fit a straight line to a wavy curve, with online gradient descent. First, the data arrives like a trajectory: left to right, then back again. Our own run: two hundred points, four passes, step size point zero five. The line chases wherever the data is right now, and forgets the rest. Its error swings up and down, and never settles. Now the same points, shuffled. The line settles right next to the best possible fit. Shuffled, the error ends within a few percent of the best a line can do. In order, it swings between about one and three times that. Same data, same model. The only difference is the order. Now imagine that with a network of millions of weights, on a whole game.

29.title: The fixes
29.text: So how do we fix the order? Experience replay: store, shuffle, and sample mini batches. Replay does double duty: it breaks the correlation, and it reuses each sample many times. Dyna-style planning does something similar, with samples from a learned model. Better optimisers help too, like momentum. So do better online algorithms, like eligibility traces. And then there's the vanilla trick: eight cores, eight simulations in parallel. Eight independent streams. Solved by engineering, not by maths. Totally legit. Eight streams also means eight times the data, for every second you wait.

29.title: The triad, again
29.text: But look at what DQN combines. A neural network. Bootstrapped targets. And a replay buffer full of old policies. Function approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy. The deadly triad, all three. Is this a sane thing to do? Researchers measured it, in twenty eighteen. Unbounded divergence turned out to be rare. More common: the values blow up early, then come back down. They called it soft divergence. Soft divergence still hurts. While the values are wrong, the policy built on them is wrong too. So yes, the guarantees die. But in practice, the patient usually survives.

29.title: Good-enough optima
29.text: So why does it work at all? It converges to a local optimum that's good enough. The downsides: it's very sensitive to where you start. Which optimum you land in depends a lot on luck, and on where you start. And it nails the problem it trained on, but doesn't generalise. The original DQN trained a separate network for every Atari game. Feed it lots of data from one narrow region, and it becomes an expert on exactly that region. Later work trained one model across many games.

29.title: A good start
29.text: About that starting point. A random network is usually bad, because most of the space is bad. Now imagine that a good starting point fell from the sky. Then you search aggressively around it. That's the idea behind imitation learning: start from a human's good policy, and improve from there. In many real projects that's exactly the plan: a human demonstrates first, and the agent takes over. Start well, and half the battle is won. And even then, the training curves take millions of episodes, and stay noisy.

29.title: Target networks
29.text: Back to the triad. TD chases its own tail: change the weights, and the target moves too. The fix is a target network. A frozen copy of the weights, used only to compute the targets. Train the main network for a few thousand steps against a target that stands still. Then copy the weights over. Think of a dog chasing its own tail. Now tie the tail to a post for a while. You can't backpropagate from one network into the other. So you copy the weights, every so often. That's the trick. It breaks the feedback loop at the heart of the triad. Copy too often, and the target moves again. Copy too rarely, and you learn from stale values. A frozen target turns each stretch of training back into ordinary regression.

29.title: Double DQN
29.text: Remember double Q-learning? Q-learning was too optimistic, so we split it in two. DQN already has two networks. So the online network picks the best next action, and the frozen one scores it. That's double DQN. Same idea, almost for free. The online network is fresh, so it picks well. The frozen one is independent enough to score honestly. And in that twenty eighteen study, the double versions blew up far less often. They looked at the largest values each agent predicted. Plain Q-learning blew up most often.

29.title: Recap
29.text: Correlated data: shuffle it, or run in parallel. Moving targets: freeze them. Optimism: split the job in two. None of these is a proof. Together, they made deep Q-learning work in practice. Next time: not all samples are born equal. Plus a few tricks that make deep networks fit reinforcement learning better.

30.title: Dogs, cats and wolves
30.text: Not all samples are born equal. DQN samples its replay buffer uniformly. Every memory has the same chance. In class, I used a classifier for dogs, cats and wolves. Tons of dog and cat photos. Very few wolves. Your model is already good at dogs and cats. On wolves, it's badly wrong. So where should you spend your energy? On the wolves. Prioritised replay does exactly that. A sample's priority is the size of its last TD error. In practice, you sample by priority, and keep updating each priority as the errors change. A simple idea. Nothing fancy. And it doesn't have to be wolves. Any rare, surprising transition gets more attention.

30.title: The numbers
30.text: Some numbers. A buffer with forty five dogs, forty five cats and ten wolves. The errors: point one on dogs, point two on cats, and two on wolves. Uniform sampling picks a wolf ten percent of the time. By priority: about sixty percent. So the wolves get sampled six times more often. The model spends its time where it's wrong. Ten wolves out of a hundred, and they get most of the attention. The catch: now the samples don't match what the agent really sees. Even more off-policy. Importance weights fix part of that. Samples that got picked a lot count a little less.

30.title: Multi-step targets
30.text: Next: multi-step targets. Take n real rewards, then bootstrap, with the double Q trick. The meaning: follow your behaviour for n steps, then act greedily. Still a policy improvement. Just a less greedy one. It trades bias against variance, and leans less on bootstrapping. On-policy for n steps, then greedy. That's a well-defined target, and still a good one. Less bootstrapping, fewer explosions. Researchers saw it: bigger n, safer values. In that same study, three steps blew up much less often than one, and ten steps less than three.

30.title: Inductive bias
30.text: Now the other direction: make the network fit reinforcement learning. Copying architectures from supervised learning is a start. But we shouldn't stop there. The question for reinforcement learning: which inductive biases help an agent that acts? Deep learning's big wins came from the right inductive bias. Convolutions for images, because a cat looks like a cat anywhere in the picture. Gating, as in LSTMs, for long memory. So which layers for your agent? Convolution only if the input has spatial structure, like Atari pixels. A feature vector has none. Sequences? Recurrent networks. Fully connected layers are fine for finding relations among features. And attention, lately, does great everywhere.

30.title: Dueling networks
30.text: One architecture was made just for reinforcement learning: the dueling network. Split q into two parts: how good is this state, v, and how much better is each action, the advantage. Then add them back up, and you still get q. The state value gets an update from every action. So it learns faster. On a straight, empty road, every action is about the same. The state value carries it. Learn the state once, and the differences separately. Less to learn for every action. And the advantages tell you which action is best, which is all the policy needs. A small change to the network, and often a big change to learning.

30.title: Capacity
30.text: Capacity. In supervised learning, more data plus a bigger network usually means better results. In reinforcement learning, bigger networks typically do better too. But they're also more prone to the deadly triad. So scale up, but watch your values for explosions. More capacity isn't free. It's one more thing to

30.title: The wall
30.text: tune. And generalisation can bite. Picture a maze with a wall. On one side of the wall, you're one step from the goal. On the other side, it's a long way around. Nearby states, very different values. A network smooths over the wall, and the values leak through it. This is called leakage propagation. Errors leak through the wall, and then they spread. Monte Carlo sees how episodes really end, so it learns there's no way through. But it still underestimates near the wall. TD keeps telling itself: I'm almost there. And its error grows, step by step. Monte Carlo leaks too. But it doesn't feed on its own leaks. And that's not a bug in one algorithm. It's what generalisation does near a sharp edge.

30.title: Learning about many things
30.text: Behind the triad and the leakage is the same problem: the wrong generalisation. Better representations help. One way to get them: learn about many things at once. Predict the values of other policies. Predict the next observations. Predict signals besides the reward. Every extra prediction shapes a better shared representation. Almost for free. Even if you only care about one reward, learning about many things helps. That's where module eleven picks up, later in the series.

30.title: Module eight, done
30.text: And that's module eight, done. Three modules ago, Bit couldn't act. Now he acts, generalises, and trains deep networks without blowing up. Mostly. Correlated data, moving targets, optimism and leakage. Each one has a fix, and none of the fixes is a guarantee. And it all combines with the tricks from earlier: traces, double learning, and replay. Next module: planning. Bit learns a model of the world, and starts to imagine. See you there.

31.title: Recorded forever
31.text: I'm recording this. So everything silly I say is saved forever. Well, at least two years. Forever or two years, whichever comes first. Module nine: planning, models and search. A quick recap. So far, we told Bit nothing about the world. It tried things, got rewards, and learned values. Remember the ninety nine and the hundred gold coins? Bit learned they're related. But what gold actually is, it has no idea. Close to its data, it does fine. Far from its data, it can't extrapolate. But we know a tool that's great at exactly that. Show it data, and it finds the hidden pattern. Supervised learning.

31.title: Best of both
31.text: So far we had two worlds. Dynamic programming: hand me the model, and I'll solve it. But on big problems, it explodes. Model-free learning: assume nothing, and learn values straight from experience. What if we take the best of both? Learn a model from experience, then plan with it. That's model-based reinforcement learning. The loop changes a little. Experience no longer teaches the values directly. It teaches a model, and the model teaches the values. Careful with words, by the way. Until now, the model usually meant the policy. Today, a model means a model of the world.

31.title: Why bother
31.text: Let's start with the downside. We added a stage. And what happens when you add stages? I see engineers in the audience. More failure points. The model can be wrong, and then the values built on top of it are wrong too. Two sources of error instead of one. Now the upsides. Supervised learning is very good at this job. And many models can tell you how confident they are. Low confidence somewhere interesting? Maybe invest more effort there. Sounds familiar? That was the bandits. And the big one: fewer real samples. Simulating a thousand poker games is cheap. Running a robot is not. A robot run needs a robot, a room, sensors and people. On a bad day, the robot breaks. Asking a model costs a few chips and some electricity.

31.title: What's a model
31.text: Formally, a model approximates the dynamics of the MDP, with weights we call eta. Give it a state and an action, and it predicts the reward and the next state. Can every world be learned like this? In class, I played a game with a student. I say numbers, you guess the next one. The trick: every new run is longer than everything before it. Whatever pattern you learn, the next run breaks it. No function keeps up. Luckily, the real world lives in R n. It's a metric space, and there it works. This is my course, so I decide what's true.

31.title: Dynamics, not policy
31.text: So learning a model is supervised learning. The inputs: a state and an action. The targets: the reward and the next state. The data is our experience. A history is one episode. Experience is many of them. Notice what we're learning here. Not the policy. The dynamics. Many people get this wrong. Predicting two outputs at once is painful regression. So we train two models: one for the reward, one for the next state. That's all the genius.

31.title: Dynamics vs desires
31.text: Here's why keeping them apart matters. The reward depends on what I want. The transition does not. Teach a robot one task, and along the way it learns how the world moves. Now ask it for a different task. Do you learn the dynamics again? No. You got them for free. Chess puzzles teach you how the pieces move, and that carries over to a full game. Some worlds are deterministic, like chess. Some are not, like ice skating. Trust me on this one. You fall, randomly, and hard.

31.title: Into the wall
31.text: The simplest model predicts the expected next state. And expectations can bite. Say an action sends you left of a wall or right of it, half the time each. The expected next state? Right inside the wall. On a grid, the expectation can land half a cell away. A place that doesn't exist. Linear models suffer less here. A straight line has fewer ways to surprise you. And with linear values, the expected next state even gives the right expected value.

31.title: Expectations lie
31.text: Another one. A world gives minus a million once, plus a million once, and zero nine hundred and ninety eight times. The expectation: zero. The model did its job faithfully. And it's still useless. Sample one of those millions, and everything shifts. So make the model stochastic. Feed it some noise, and let it predict a next state from that noise. If you've met diffusion models, it's the same spirit. Start from noise, and shape it into something that fits the condition. A stochastic model can be chained, step after step, even when it's non-linear. It just adds some noise along the way.

31.title: The A-B table
31.text: The humblest model of all is a table. Count how often each state and action led where, and average the rewards. The A B example, eight episodes. A, zero, B, zero. Then six times B, one. And once, B, zero. From A, we always went to B, with reward zero. From B, reward one six times out of eight. Seventy five percent. That's a whole model, learned by counting. No action choices in this one. Things just happen. Next time, we plan with it. And find out it can lie to us.

32.title: What planning means
32.text: Planning. A word that means different things to different people. Ask someone in robotics, and planning is close to prediction. Ask a mechanical engineer, and it's closer to optimisation. For us, planning means spending compute to improve values and policies, without touching the real world. Dynamic programming is the best example we've seen so far. But it assumed someone handed us the model. Today, nobody hands us anything. We learn the model ourselves, and plan with what we learned.

32.title: Option one: DP
32.text: Option one: learn the model, then run your favourite dynamic programming on it. Value iteration, policy iteration, whatever you like. But remember the tree. Dynamic programming sweeps every branch, level after level. On big problems, it explodes. Most of those branches you'll never visit anyway. Why pay for them? Option one also needs a full model, with a probability for each possible next state. Often, all we can learn is a model we can sample

32.title: Option two: sample
32.text: from. Option two is simple and powerful. Use the model only to generate samples. Imagine experience. Ask the model what happens next, again and again. Then run plain model-free learning on the imagined data. Monte Carlo, SARSA, Q-learning. The real world gave us a little data. The model turns it into as much data as we want. A model, in other words, is just a simulator you learned yourself. Cheap to run, and as honest as the data it came from.

32.title: A and B, imagined
32.text: Back to A and B. We built our table model by counting the eight real episodes. Now we sample eight imagined episodes from it, and run Monte Carlo on those. In our draw, A came out at one, and B at point eight seven five. From the real data, Monte Carlo says V of A is zero. It saw A exactly once, and that time it got nothing. So which one is right? Neither. Under the model, the answer is point seven five. The dynamics look perfect, and the values are still off. More samples fix it. With twenty thousand imagined episodes, V of A lands on point seven six. The law of large numbers, again. Just because you learned that law long ago doesn't mean you forgot it. It means you had lots of time to practise it. So even a model that's exactly right about the data can give wrong values, simply because we sampled too little from it.

32.title: The limits
32.text: Now the limits. Give me an imperfect model, which is most of the time, and planning can hand you a suboptimal policy. So I stop promising you a global optimum. I don't even promise a local one. Your performance is capped by the model. Non-linear dynamics with a linear model? Sample forever. You'll never get there. Model-based learning is only as good as the estimated model. It sits in the middle, and if it's bad, everything after it is bad. You can check a model like any supervised model: train, test, validation. But that only covers the things you've already seen. And in reinforcement learning, there are always things you haven't seen yet. That's the whole game.

32.title: Three ways out
32.text: So how do we live with a wrong model? Approach one: when the model is wrong, fall back to model-free learning. Approach two: reason about the model's uncertainty. Bayesian methods, if you've met them. Approach three: combine model-based and model-free learning in one algorithm. That's next episode. In practice, you rarely know the model is wrong. You find out when reality disagrees with it.

32.title: The always-wrong trader
32.text: Now a fun question. Can a model's mistakes actually help you learn? You want to get rich. So you build an algorithmic trading model. And it's wrong every single time. When you should buy, it says sell. When you should sell, it says buy. A hundred percent of the time. Good model, or bad model? Excellent model. Do the opposite, and you're rich. Extreme, I know. But it makes the point. Less extreme: a model that's wrong in a consistent way still tells you something. Errors you can predict are information.

32.title: Over the hill
32.text: A less extreme case. Picture a loss with a hill in the way. The best point sits behind it. To get there, things must look worse for a while. TD, with a limited number of tries, prefers not to climb. Bellman promises you'll get there if you try infinitely often. We never do. Now and then, a slightly wrong model, plus some luck, says: why not try over there? And it lands you past the hill. That's rare, and it's luck. The deliberate fixes are simulated annealing, which comes from heating and cooling metals, and population methods. Simulated annealing: heat a metal, and its atoms jump around. Cool it slowly, and they settle into a better arrangement. Jumping is the point.

32.title: Science → art
32.text: So: models turn a little real data into a lot of imagined data. That's the whole point. Asking a model is cheap. The real world is not. Their weakness: they cap you. A bad model means bad values. The first lectures of this course were science: promises, optimality, proofs. From here on, it's more of an art. Guess, think, try. Next time: the best of both worlds. Bit learns and dreams at the same time. It's called Dyna.

33.title: Why a model
33.text: Why do we even bother with a model? Not because it's more accurate. A model-free learner has fewer places to break. One reason only. Real samples are expensive, and the model saves them. So should I average the model and the real world, half and half? Then every imagined sample costs me a real one. I saved nothing. Better: for every real step, take many imagined steps. Nine imagined ones for each real one, and I get ten times the updates. Of course, that only helps if the imagined steps are any good. Early on, they aren't. We'll get to that.

33.title: The Dyna loop
33.text: That's Dyna. Real experience does two jobs. It updates the values directly, like plain Q-learning. And it teaches the model. The model then generates imagined experience, which updates the same values again. Real or imagined, the update looks exactly the same. The values don't care where a sample came from. Draw it as a loop: act, see, learn. And next to it, a second loop that never touches the world: imagine, learn.

33.title: Dyna-Q in code
33.text: What I love about reinforcement learning: the core of the code is tiny. Dyna Q is about twenty lines. Pick an action, epsilon greedy. Take it. See the next state and the reward. Update Q exactly as in Q-learning. Then store what happened in the model: this state and this action led there, with this reward. And then plan. N times: pick a state you've already seen, an action you already took there, ask the model, and update Q again. That's it. The rest is bookkeeping: storing the model, and picking samples from it.

33.title: Only seen states
33.text: Why only states we've already seen? Because a model can't invent new states. Or worse, it invents them by mistake. In chess, a white pawn can never stand on the first row. Pawns start on the second row, and only move forward. A sloppy model might predict exactly that. So we only plan from places we've actually been.

33.title: The maze, our runs
33.text: Does it work? We ran Dyna Q on a small maze. Six by nine, a few walls, a start and a goal. Thirty runs each. With no planning at all, that's plain Q-learning, the second episode still takes about six hundred and thirty steps. With five planning steps per real step: about a hundred and fifty. With fifty: thirty seven. By episode ten, five or fifty planning steps both walk the maze in about seventeen steps. Without planning: still about a hundred and forty. Why so fast? When the goal is first reached, only one state learns about it. With planning, that news spreads backwards through the whole maze before the next episode starts. Same real experience. The imagined steps did the

33.title: Growing the planning
33.text: rest. One thing I do in practice. At the start, the model is awful. So why trust it? I let the number of planning steps grow. Start small, even zero, and increase it as the model improves. In our maze, growing from zero to fifty planning steps reached the same seventeen steps by episode ten. Fixed at fifty did even better early on, because our model is just a table of what happened. It's never wrong about what it saw. With a learned, noisy model, waiting matters much more. The best numbers for that schedule? That's a riddle. Tune them for your problem.

33.title: A shortcut opens
33.text: But a model is also a prior. And priors resist change. We ran a maze that gets easier. Halfway through, a shortcut opens in the wall. Plain Dyna Q keeps taking the old road: about eighteen steps to the goal, before and after. Its model says the wall is closed, and it never checks. Dyna Q plus adds a small bonus for trying things it hasn't tried in a while. It finds the shortcut: about twelve steps. The bonus isn't free. Before the change, Dyna Q plus needed about twenty steps per goal, against eighteen. Exploration always costs something. When the world changes, a model-free learner just updates. A model-based learner must first fix its model, and only then its values.

33.title: The boat
33.text: A real example. I worked on an autonomous boat. A day of sea trials costs tens of thousands of shekels. A big ship carries the small boat out. A crew of six or seven. And someone has to sit in a beach cafe and make sure it all works. That's me. So we built a physics simulation of the boat. A digital twin. Not my favourite term. Simulating physics at high resolution is expensive too. But it's still tens of times cheaper than a day at sea. And the sea is a terrible place. Turbulence, temperature, jammed GPS. Reinforcement learning doesn't need to solve the turbulence. Give the boat a goal, and enough practice. That's what a model is for. An expensive world, swapped for a cheap one, as long as the cheap one is good enough.

33.title: Learn and dream
33.text: Dyna, in one line: real steps teach the model, and imagined steps teach the values. Sink in more compute, and learn more from every real step. That matters most when real data is slow, expensive or unsafe. Robots. Cars. Boats. Next time: wait a second. Isn't the replay buffer already a model?

34.title: Two boxes
34.text: Old textbooks sorted algorithms into two neat boxes. Model-free: update values or policies, with no model of the dynamics. Model-based: learn transitions and rewards, then plan with them. Then everyone started storing experience in a replay buffer. And the boxes got blurry. Today: is a replay buffer a model? And if it is, why would anyone build anything fancier?

34.title: The buffer is a model
34.text: Think about what replay actually does. Store real transitions. Later, sample them, and run model-free updates on them. That's Dyna. The buffer is the model. A non-parametric one: it doesn't predict, it remembers. Dyna asks the model: given this state and action, what happens? Replay just pulls out a whole remembered transition. Same benefit. Many updates on old data, for every new step in the world. And we already used it. DQN, back in module seven, was Dyna in disguise.

34.title: Replay vs Dyna
34.text: We checked on our maze. Q-learning with replay, five replayed updates per real step, against Dyna Q with five planning steps. Second episode: about two hundred and ten steps with replay, a hundred and fifty with the model. By episode ten, both are at about seventeen. In a small, deterministic table world, a perfect model and a replay buffer give the same answer for every state and action they've seen. So why the gap early on? Replay draws transitions as often as they happened. Our model picks seen pairs evenly. Different information, slightly different paths. And the same answer only holds when the model is perfect. A learned model has errors, and there the two part ways. Could those errors make learning better? Unlikely, if you only imagine transitions from states and actions you've actually tried. Then a buffer is just as good.

34.title: Markov, and poker
34.text: Now a confession. We assume Markov: the present state is enough. So why remember where we came from? Markov is a lovely theoretical idea. In practice, it's often better to know more. More information never hurts. Engineering costs aside. Poker. Technically, the cards in your hand decide your next move. But remember what the others did at the table, and you might learn some psychology on the way. Who bluffs, who folds early, who gets nervous. None of that is in your cards. All of it is in the history.

34.title: Fill, use, empty
34.text: How do I sample from a buffer? Honestly, nothing fancy. Fill the buffer. Use it. Empty it. The most naive thing there is. There are papers showing that smarter sampling helps, and I don't dismiss them for a second. My two cents: fill, use, empty. It works great too. It depends on so many things. The size of the buffer, the problem, how often you update. Try it on yours. And replay gives you something else. The same data, seen again in a new context. A bit like epochs in deep learning.

34.title: Memory vs compute
