34.text: A common story. Engineers make the buffer bigger, and learning gets faster. What fun. So they make it bigger again. Every trick has a limit. The early speed-up flattens out, and you're left holding lots of useless memory. It's a classic trade. Spend memory to save compute, or spend compute to save memory. And on that axis, models and buffers differ. Querying a buffer is cheap, but it grows with its capacity. A big generative model can be expensive to sample, but it stays the same size. So, a rule of thumb: a big buffer is good. But the returns diminish. Watch for the point where more memory stops buying you speed.

34.title: What only a model can do
34.text: So why bother with a parametric model at all? Because it can answer questions a buffer can't. Plan for action selection: ask about actions you could take in the future. Counterfactuals: ask about actions you could have taken in the past, but didn't. The road not taken. Plan backwards: which states could have led to this outcome? And plan in jumps, at different time scales. A buffer can only replay what happened. A model can imagine what didn't. That's planning with things that never happened. Powerful, and also exactly where a model can fool

34.title: It's all ratios
34.text: you. Is asking the model worth it? It's all about ratios. Say a model call costs ten milliseconds, and a real step costs a hundred. Nine model calls instead of one real step, and you're saving. Eleven, and you're wasteful. For real robots and boats, the ratio is huge, and models win easily. For a board game you can simulate for free? Much less so. And don't forget: the model must be trained first, and that costs real samples too. Model-free pays per step. Model-based pays up front. So before you build a model, ask yourself one question: how much does a real sample cost me?

34.title: Remember vs imagine
34.text: So: a replay buffer is a model too. A simple, cheap, honest one. A learned model costs more. But it can imagine what never happened. Use the buffer when the past is enough. Build a model when you need to ask about what never happened. Next time, we use a model differently. Not to improve values everywhere, but to choose the very next move. Look before you leap.

35.title: Plan for now
35.text: So far, the model improved our values everywhere. Today, we plan only for the state we're in, right now. The states you'll meet in the next few moves are a tiny slice of the world. You can get them much more right than the whole map. And a wrong model here mostly leads to some interesting exploration, not to bad updates everywhere. Think of a chess player. They don't evaluate every position in chess. Just the ones that can follow from the board in front of them.

35.title: Forward search
35.text: Forward search. Build a tree with your current state at the root, and use the model to look ahead. Imagine the game in your head. You play against your own model of the world. It takes a state and an action, and gives back the next state. No need to solve the whole MDP. Just the smaller one that starts from here. I like to call it shadowing. Like a shadow that follows you around. Except this shadow runs ahead of

35.title: Expectimax explodes
35.text: you. With a perfect model, you can compute the best action exactly. An expectimax tree: take the max over your actions, and average over the world's answers. The catch: the tree grows like states times actions, to the power of the depth. Tic-tac-toe has three hundred sixty two thousand eight hundred and eighty ways to fill the board, move by move. Go has three hundred sixty one first moves. Four moves deep, that's about seventeen billion lines. And the world often answers at random, so every action branches again into many possible next states. So we sample instead.

35.title: Simulate whole episodes
35.text: Simulation-based search. From the current state, simulate whole episodes with the model, and run model-free learning on them. The simplest version: for each action, simulate K episodes, average the returns, and pick the best action. Before, we used the model like TD: one step, one prediction. Now we use it like Monte Carlo: a whole imagined episode, all the way to the end. And if the imagined road turns out bad in reality? You still learned something important. You thought it was good, and now you know better. The cost: for every action, many imagined episodes. Each one is cheap, but they add up.

35.title: MCTS in four steps
35.text: Now the star of the show: Monte Carlo tree search. It sits at the heart of AlphaGo. Keep a tree of the states you've visited, with a value for each action. Every simulation has four steps. Select: walk down the tree, picking actions by their values. Expand: add one new node. Roll out: play to the end with a simple policy, often just random moves. Back up: update every value along the path with the result. When time runs out, stop searching, and play the best action at the root. Which one is best? Usually the one with the most visits, not the highest average. A few lucky playouts can fool an average. Many visits are much harder to fool. The rollout doesn't need to be smart. It just needs to finish the game, so you get a result.

35.title: Monte Carlo in two layers
35.text: The way I like to think about it: Monte Carlo, in two layers. Layer one is the Monte Carlo you know. Start from a board, and play until the game ends. Win, lose or draw. Layer two: where do you start? Pick, at random, one of the boards you've already seen, and play it out from there. In class: a cute new robot faces a chess board. Fifty moves later, the game ends. Next, it pulls out a board it has already seen, and plays from there. Two random processes, one on top of the other. And the chance of repeating a long line exactly is tiny, so every playout teaches you something new.

35.title: One dense cloud
35.text: Why does this work so well? It builds one big, dense cloud of samples around where you are. Classic sampling gives you lots of small clouds, spread over a huge space. And dense data is exactly what supervised models love. That's one reason tree search fits so nicely inside model-based reinforcement learning. And it's fast for the same reason. It spends its effort on what matters for the next move, not on the far corners of the game. Think of a tourist with one free afternoon. You don't study the map of the whole city. You study the streets around your hotel.

35.title: Half the world
35.text: The weakness? A silly example. A first screen: choose right, and you enter one game. Choose left, and you enter a different game. Start on the right, keep searching inside the right game, and you'll never see the left one. You just lost half the world. Plain Monte Carlo would stumble into the left side now and then. Tree search builds on itself. And one more sad fact. You work hard, you grow a beautiful tree, you make one single decision, and most of the tree dies. Only the branch you took survives.

35.title: Pros and cons
35.text: The advantages: highly selective, best first. It evaluates states on the fly. It only needs samples, so a black box model is fine. And you can stop it any time. But the tree itself is a lookup table. It doesn't generalise between similar states. The fix comes from earlier in this course: put a learned value function on top of the tree, so it can extrapolate between states. Next time: how should the tree choose which branch to explore? Spoiler: bandits. They're back.

36.title: Which branch?
36.text: Inside the tree, every simulation has to choose: which action do I try next? Always the best one so far, and you might miss a better branch. Always at random, and you waste your budget on silly moves. Sounds familiar? Explore or exploit. Our old friend, the multi-armed bandit. Every node is a little room full of slot machines. Pull an arm, get a simulated result, update your average.

36.title: A bandit per node
36.text: UCT, upper confidence trees, treats every node as its own bandit. Each action is an arm. Score each arm by its average return, plus a bonus that grows when it's been tried rarely. Square root of log big N, over small n. Pick the arm with the highest upper bound. Go down. Repeat at the next node. It's the same UCB we met in module two, with Hoeffding behind it. There, the arms were slot machines. Here, they're moves. So the policy that grows the tree changes from one simulation to the next. It learns while it searches. Log big N grows slowly with the visits to the parent. Small n counts the visits to this arm. An arm that's rarely tried gets a big bonus.

36.title: Two policies
36.text: That gives us two policies. The tree policy, which improves as the search runs. And the rollout policy, which stays fixed. Often, just random. The tree policy is smart near the root. The rollout policy just finishes the game, so we get a result to back up. In the first AlphaGo, the rollouts came from a small, fast policy. In AlphaZero, there are no rollouts at all. More on that next time. Why random rollouts at all? Because they're cheap. And averaged over many games, even random play says something about a position.

36.title: UCT vs random
36.text: We built one. UCT for tic-tac-toe, with random rollouts. Two hundred games against a random player, for each budget. Ten simulations per move: it wins seventy eight percent of games, and loses seventeen. Fifty simulations: eighty five percent wins, four percent losses. A thousand simulations: ninety seven and a half percent wins, and not a single loss. The rest are draws. Against a random player, draws mean the random player got lucky. Not that our search was clever. Look at the jump from ten to fifty. Five times the budget, and the losses fall from seventeen percent to four.

36.title: Find the win
36.text: Now a position where X can win in one move. Five empty squares, one of them wins. With five simulations, it finds the winning square twenty percent of the time. That's a pure guess: one in five. With fifty simulations: sixty nine percent. With one hundred: ninety six percent. With two hundred: every time. Early on, the bonus pushes it to try everything. With enough simulations, the averages win the argument. That's the bandit trade-off in miniature: spend some simulations checking everything, then commit to what works.

36.title: Where the time goes
36.text: From the empty board, with two thousand simulations, where does the search spend its time? The centre gets four hundred and seventy six visits. The corners, about two hundred and twenty each. The edges, about a hundred and sixty. The visit counts are the answer. The most visited move is the one to play. Centre first, like every child learns eventually. Nobody told it about the centre. It found that out from nothing but random games and

36.title: UCT vs UCT
36.text: counting. Then we let two UCT players meet, a thousand simulations each. Forty games. Forty draws. Tic-tac-toe is a draw with perfect play. Both of them found it, from random rollouts and a bandit formula. Two perfect players, and no winner. Like most arguments about the best programming language. Against each other, they can't exploit any mistakes, because neither of them makes one.

36.title: Regret in a dream
36.text: Now something slightly strange. Why did we like upper confidence bounds in the first place? Because exploring costs real reward. Inside the tree, nothing is real. A bad simulated move costs nothing but compute. So minimising regret inside the simulations isn't quite the right goal. What we really want is the best decision at the root. People study this as choosing which computation to run. UCT works very well in practice anyway. Theory and practice, as usual, are not always on speaking terms. When does the bandit view still make sense? When simulations are expensive. Every simulation spent on a bad move is one not spent on a good move.

36.title: Flat vs UCT
36.text: One more comparison. Flat Monte Carlo, with two hundred simulations spread evenly over the moves, won ninety two and a half percent against the random player. UCT, with the same two hundred, won ninety five percent. Spending simulations where they matter pays off, even in a game this small. And the search never knew a single tic-tac-toe strategy. The rules, random rollouts, and one formula. Tic-tac-toe is tiny. Go is not. To scale this up, the tree needs a much better guess at each leaf than a random game. Next time: put a neural network inside the tree, let it play itself millions of times, and beat the best Go players in the world.

37.title: Why Go is hard
37.text: Go. More than two and a half thousand years old. Black and white stones on a nineteen by nineteen board. The rules are simple. Surround stones to capture them, and the player with more territory wins. The strategy is anything but simple. Classic game tree search, the kind that conquered chess, failed at Go. Too many moves, and no good way to judge a position. Go has three hundred sixty one points to play at the start, and on average about two hundred and fifty legal moves per turn. So you can't look far ahead, and you can't easily tell who's winning. Search needs both.

37.title: AlphaGo, 2016
37.text: In March twenty sixteen, DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, one of the strongest players in the world, four games to one. AlphaGo learned first from human games, then improved by playing itself, and searched with Monte Carlo tree search. Its search used two networks, one proposing moves and one judging positions, plus fast rollouts to the end. And then they asked: what if we drop the humans completely?

37.title: Self-play
37.text: The key idea: self-play. The agent plays against itself. At every position, it computes its best move. For the opponent's move, it does the same. The only bottleneck is compute. No humans needed. Self-play gives you a perfectly matched opponent, always. Never too weak, never too strong. As you improve, so does your opponent. The reward is sparse: win or lose, once, at the very end of the game. And there's no curriculum to design. Your teacher is always exactly one step ahead of you, because your teacher is you.

37.title: One network, two heads
37.text: AlphaGo Zero used one network with two heads. Give it a board. One head gives a probability for every move. The other gives a value: how likely am I to win from here? Inside the tree search, the policy head says which moves look promising, so the search tries those first. At a leaf, no random rollout. The value head simply says how good the position is. Run many simulations, then turn the visit counts at the root into a policy. More visits, more probability. Those visit counts are smarter than the raw network. That's the whole trick: search turns a good policy into a better one. Early in a self-play game, it picks moves in proportion to their visits, to explore. Later on, it plays the most visited move.

37.title: The training loop
37.text: Play a whole game this way, move after move, until someone wins. Then train the network. The policy head learns to predict what the search chose. The value head learns to predict who won. A better network makes a better search. A better search makes better training data. And round and round it goes. Look familiar? It's policy iteration. The search improves the policy, and the network learns to imitate the improvement. Each move used sixteen hundred simulations. About point four seconds of thinking. Fewer simulations than you'd expect, for a game this big. The network makes every simulation count.

37.title: Results
37.text: The results, from DeepMind's paper in Nature, twenty seventeen. No human games at all. Just the rules. After three days of self-play, AlphaGo Zero beat the version that had beaten Lee Sedol. A hundred games to zero. After forty days, it was stronger than every earlier version. In those first three days, it played about four point nine million games against itself. No opening books, no human games, no hand-made features. The board, the rules, and itself.

37.title: The search
37.text: So what made it so strong? People asked three questions. One: the search. The network on its own, just playing its first instinct, was rated about three thousand and fifty five Elo. With tree search on top: about five thousand one hundred and eighty five. Same network. Searching at play time was worth more than two thousand Elo points. The raw network on its own sat a little below AlphaGo Fan, the version that first beat a professional player. The search did the rest.

37.title: No humans, AlphaZero
37.text: Two: the architecture. One residual network for both policy and value, instead of two separate networks, was a clear part of the gain in their comparisons. Three: human data. Starting from zero, with no human games, it ended up stronger than the versions that learned from humans first. Remember module eight: a network that learns its own representation. Here, that pays off in full. Then AlphaZero did the same for chess and shogi too. One algorithm, just the rules. In the paper's runs: nine hours of training for chess, twelve for shogi, thirty four for Go.

37.title: Module nine, done
37.text: Everything in this module, in one system. A learned evaluation, a model to search with, Monte Carlo, bandits in the tree, and self-play to make the data. One footnote. AlphaZero was given the rules. Its model was perfect. When the model has to be learned too, everything we said about wrong models comes back. A later system, MuZero, took on exactly that. And one thing to keep from all of this: a policy is good. A policy plus search is better. And that's module nine, done. Next module, we forget values for a while, and learn the policy directly. Policy gradients.

38.title: The long way around
38.text: Module ten: policy gradients and actor critics. Quick recap. So far we always took the long way around. Learn values, then read a policy off them. Or learn a model, plan with it, and get a policy. Even the question of which policy is better, we answered with values. Policy pi beats policy pi prime if its value is at least as high in every state. And remember the flips? A tiny error in the values, and the greedy policy suddenly jumps to a completely different action. So today, a new idea. Why not learn the policy directly?

38.title: Three roads
38.text: There's a lovely line from Vladimir Vapnik: do not solve a more general problem as an intermediate step. Three roads lead to the same place, the optimal policy. Model-based, value-based, and policy-based. Sometimes the model is the easy part. If the dynamics are simple, a few samples teach you how the world moves. And sometimes the dynamics are a nightmare, but the best policy is simple. Always move forward, for example.

38.title: Beat the casino
38.text: A well known joke in statistics. What's the best way to beat a casino? Don't play. It sounds silly, but statistically it's the right answer. The expected value of every casino game is against the player. Poker, roulette, pick your favourite. The dynamics are anything but simple. The optimal policy? Whatever the state, do nothing. Complex world, trivial policy. In a case like that, learning a model or every value is a lot of work for

38.title: Pros and cons
38.text: nothing. The advantages. First, we optimise the true objective. For the first time, we learn exactly the thing we wanted to learn. It extends easily to huge or continuous action spaces. It can learn stochastic policies. And sometimes the policy is just simpler. The disadvantages. It can get stuck in a local optimum. The knowledge it learns can be very specific. And on its own, it doesn't squeeze every drop of information out of the data. Sound familiar? Gradient descent with backpropagation has exactly the same problems. They come from optimising over functions, not from reinforcement learning.

38.title: A policy, directly
38.text: A policy, written directly: the probability of taking action a in state s, given parameters theta. If the policy is deterministic, those probabilities are zero or one. If it's stochastic, anything in between. The same notation covers both. Now, in a fully observed MDP, there's always an optimal deterministic policy. So why would we ever want randomness? Because most problems aren't fully observed. Board games, maybe. Almost everything else, no. And with function approximation, states blur together all the time. Randomness also makes the landscape smooth, so gradients can work. And it explores for free while we learn.

38.title: The aliased corridor
38.text: Here's a small world. A corridor of five cells. Gold below the middle one, and a skull below each end. The agent only feels the walls around it. And the two grey cells feel exactly the same: a wall above, a wall below, open on both sides. A deterministic policy must do the same thing in both grey cells. Say it always goes right. From the left half, great, you reach the gold. From the right half, you step right, the corner sends you back left, and you bounce between those two cells forever. We simulated it. From a random start, the deterministic policy reaches the gold sixty percent of the time. The other forty percent, it walks back and forth until we stop it.

38.title: Flip a coin
38.text: Now flip a coin in the grey cells. Fifty percent left, fifty percent right. What's the chance you go left ten times in a row? One half to the power of ten. About one in a thousand. Left forever? Zero. In our runs, the coin-flip policy reached the gold every single time, in about three point eight steps on average. And this isn't random tie-breaking. When we learn the policy directly, the probabilities can be anything, not just fifty fifty. Whatever works best.

38.title: What we maximise
38.text: So what exactly are we maximising? Imagine you love diving. I give you a policy: every minute, go down one more metre, no matter what. Good policy? At some point you die. Call that minus infinity. Not a great dive. For episodes like a dive, we judge a policy by its expected total return from the start. That's the value of the start state. Where do we start? From a start state distribution, d zero. In chess, it's a single board. In blackjack, it's every pair of cards for you and the dealer. A lot. For tasks that never end, we use the average reward per step instead. Physicists will tell you the world isn't really continuous. The computer certainly isn't. There's always a discretisation somewhere.

38.title: The pawn nobody meets
38.text: One more strange thing. Remember the white pawn on the first row? A legal board you can never reach. A value table would eventually meet that state and learn it. This objective never will. It only sees what the start distribution can reach. In theory, that's a gap. In practice? If I want to make you the best chess player in the world, do I care that you can't solve an impossible position? No. Next time: how do we actually climb this objective? With one beautiful trick.

39.title: Climbing J
39.text: Policy gradients turn reinforcement learning into an optimisation problem. Find the theta that makes J of theta as large as possible. We'll use stochastic gradient ascent. It's gradient descent, just walking uphill. Simple, and it plays nicely with deep networks. There are other ways. Hill climbing. Simulated annealing. Genetic algorithms, which I love, and evolution strategies. More robust sometimes, but they cost more. Gradients need a smooth landscape. And stochastic policies help with exactly that. Nudge a probability a little, and the expected return changes a little.

39.title: Smooth
39.text: What does smooth mean, mathematically? A function you can differentiate as many times as you like, at every point. Polynomials are smooth. Keep differentiating, you hit zero, and zero differentiates forever. Sine is smooth too: sine, cosine, minus sine, minus cosine, and back to sine. A loop-de-loop. If you can only differentiate once, the linear approximations behave, but the way they change can go wild. Smooth means nothing explodes, anywhere. We'll ask for a bit less: differentiable almost everywhere. Everywhere except a set of size zero, like a finite or countable bunch of points. You had four years for this to settle in. Why does that matter? A gradient is a promise about the neighbourhood. If the function jumps around, the promise is worthless.

39.title: The problem
39.text: Now the problem. We want the gradient of the expected reward with respect to theta. How does that expectation even depend on theta? Only indirectly. Theta picks the actions, and the actions bring the rewards. And you can't sample a reward and differentiate it. A reward is just a number. It doesn't depend on theta at all. In module two, we already met one answer: the gradient bandit. Today, we see where it actually comes from.

39.title: The trick
39.text: Here's the trick. The score function trick. Write the expectation as a sum over actions: probability of the action times its reward. Theta lives only in the probabilities. Take the gradient. Then multiply and divide by the probability. The gradient of pi divided by pi is just the gradient of log pi. And what's left is an expectation again. The gradient of the expected reward equals the expected reward times the gradient of log pi. An expectation is something we can sample. Take an action, see the reward, multiply. That's REINFORCE, from Ronald Williams, nineteen ninety two.

39.title: Why log π is easy
39.text: Why can we compute the gradient of log pi? Because pi returns a probability. A single number. It comes straight out of theta, so you know exactly how it moves when theta moves. A log of a number, and a derivative. Nothing scary. Intuition for the update: increase the probability of actions that got high rewards. Decrease the rest. In expectation, that's the true gradient. It's a trick worth stealing, by the way. It shows up all over machine learning, whenever you need a gradient through a random choice.

39.title: Our check
39.text: We checked it. A three armed bandit with a softmax policy. We know the exact gradient, so we can compare. With ten samples, the estimate is a mess. Two of the three components even point the wrong way. With a hundred, it's in the neighbourhood. With a thousand, close. With a hundred thousand, it's off by only a few thousandths. Unbiased, but noisy. That's the story of this whole module. Right on average, and all over the place on any single try.

39.title: Softmax
39.text: A softmax policy: each action gets a preference, and the probability is proportional to e to the preference. The gradient of its log is neat: the gradient of the chosen action's preference, minus the average gradient over all actions. So the chosen action goes up, and everything else shares the cost. Scaled by how good the reward was. Notice something. If every reward is positive, the chosen action always goes up, even a bad one. The good ones just go up faster.

39.title: Baselines
39.text: Now a gift from the maths. Subtract any baseline b that doesn't depend on the action, and the expected gradient doesn't change. Why? The baseline times the sum of all the probability gradients. And the probabilities always sum to one, so their gradients sum to zero. Does that matter? Scores of eight and nine, or eight hundred and nine hundred, rank the actions the same. Only relative scores count. But the noise is very different. Our run: a ten armed bandit where every reward sits around plus four. Two thousand runs, a thousand steps each. Without a baseline, after a thousand steps, it picks the best arm forty nine percent of the time. With the running average as a baseline: eighty three percent. Same gradient on average. Far less noise. When every action looks great, the baseline asks the right question: better than usual, or worse?

39.title: REINFORCE
39.text: So: REINFORCE. Sample an action, weigh the gradient of log pi by the reward, minus a baseline, and step uphill. It doesn't need a model. It doesn't need the reward function. It only needs samples, and a policy you can differentiate. The price: one sample is one noisy vote. You need a lot of votes. Calming that noise is what the next episodes are about. Next time: from a single step to a whole episode. The policy gradient theorem.

40.title: From bandits to episodes
40.text: Last time, one step: a bandit. Today, whole episodes, where every action changes what comes next. The idea carries over. Replace the immediate reward with the long-term return, G t, or with the action value, q. There are actually two policy gradient theorems, from Sutton and colleagues in two thousand. One for the average return per episode, and one for the average reward per step. The episodic one says: the gradient is the expected sum, over every step, of three things multiplied together: gamma to the t, q, and the gradient of log pi at that step.

40.title: A trajectory
40.text: Here's why it works. Take a whole trajectory: a start state, an action, a reward, a next state, an action, and so on. Its probability is a long product. The chance of the start state, times pi of the first action, times the chance of the next state, times pi of the next action. The score function trick still holds for whole trajectories. The gradient of the expected return is the expected return times the gradient of the log of that probability. And the log of a product is a sum of logs. That's what makes everything fall apart nicely. Products are painful to differentiate. Sums are easy. Every step gets its own little term.

40.title: The dynamics drop out
40.text: Look at the terms. The start state probability. The transition probabilities. Do any of them depend on theta? No. Their gradients are zero. Only the policy terms survive. The gradient becomes the return times the sum of the gradients of log pi along the way. So policy gradients don't need to know the dynamics. A little surprising, right? Shouldn't we know how our actions move the world? Remember from the very first lecture: the reward is not part of the dynamics. Dynamics is physics. We want the ball in the basket. Physics doesn't care what we want.

40.title: From t onwards
40.text: All the dependencies in a sequential problem hide inside the dynamics. Once those terms drop out, what's left separates, step by step, for a fixed policy. One more step of algebra. An action at time t can't change rewards that came before it. So each step only needs the return from that step onwards: G t. And the expected G t, given the state and action, is exactly q. That's the theorem.

40.title: 100 candies
40.text: In practice, we sample. Play a whole episode, then for every step, nudge theta by G t times the gradient of log pi. Notice we use the real G t here, not an estimate. We played to the end, so we know it. Why guess when you know the answer? It's like someone telling you: there are a hundred candies in this bag. And you say, no, no, I'd rather guess how many. No matter where we wander in this course, we come back to the same building blocks. With one step, this looks like TD. With the full return, it's Monte Carlo. For the record: if a stranger in the street offers you a bag of candies, better not take it. That's what they taught me.

40.title: Dropping γᵗ
40.text: Typically, people also drop the gamma to the t factor. In long episodes, it shrinks the signal from later steps almost to nothing. That's okay-ish. It's like pretending, at every step, that the episode could have started right there. Or, if you prefer, a slightly biased gradient. Many implementations you'll find do exactly this: keep the discount inside the return, and drop it from the update.

40.title: The short corridor
40.text: Let's run it. The short corridor, a little example from Sutton and Barto. Three cells, then the goal. Minus one for every step. All three cells look the same to the agent. And in the middle one, the actions are switched. Right takes you left, and left takes you right. We computed every policy exactly. Go right with probability ninety five percent, and it takes forty four steps on average. Go mostly left: eighty two. The best policy goes right fifty nine percent of the time, and needs about eleven point seven steps. Stochastic again. No deterministic policy comes close.

40.title: REINFORCE learns it
40.text: Now REINFORCE, learning that probability from scratch. A hundred runs, a thousand episodes each, starting from a poor policy that goes right nineteen percent of the time. In the first fifty episodes, it needs twenty three steps on average. By the last hundred episodes: thirteen point four. Close to the best possible, eleven point seven. Slow, but steady. Every episode is a noisy, unbiased vote for a slightly better policy. And notice what it never needed: the rule that switches the middle cell. And it never knew which cell it was in, either. To the agent, all three cells were the same. One probability had to work for all of them.

40.title: Average reward
40.text: The average reward version looks similar, with one change: subtract the global average reward, rho. Only the distance from the average matters. Rewards of eight and nine, or eight hundred and nine hundred, rank actions the same way. What hurts is the spread around the average. That's where the flips come from. So: policy gradients work on whole trajectories, without a model, using only what the policy itself controls. Next time: the noise problem. And a critic that helps the actor.

41.title: The noise
41.text: Policy gradients are unbiased. And very noisy. Let's talk about that noise. Two levers. One pays a hundred dollars now and then, and zero the rest of the time. The other pays one dollar, every single time. Pull each three times. One gave you three dollars. The other gave you zeros. Pull once more, and you might get the hundred. With so few samples, your estimates jump around. And a jump in the estimates means a jump in the policy. The flips again.

41.title: A baseline: q − v
41.text: The fix we met last time: a baseline. And the most common baseline is the value of the state, v of s. Then each step is weighted by q minus v. What does that measure? The contribution of my specific action, compared to how good the state already was. If my action is plain vanilla, q minus v is tiny, the gradient is tiny, and the policy barely moves. The update goes where the action actually mattered. And it pushes the policy, indirectly, toward states that are good in themselves. Good states tend to be stable states. And because the baseline depends only on the state, the expected gradient stays exactly the same. Variance reduction for free.

41.title: Is low variance good?
41.text: Is low variance always what you want? Not always, but often. Another bandit. Arm A pays ten dollars, every time. Arm B costs you ten dollars, but once in a thousand pulls, it pays a million. In expectation, arm B wins, by a lot. But if you walk in with a hundred dollars in your pocket, which one do you pick? Arm A. So reducing variance is sometimes a choice, not a law. But for learning, it's almost always worth it.

41.title: The critic
41.text: Where does v come from? A critic. A value function, learned by policy evaluation. Monte Carlo, or temporal differences. Nothing new. For evaluating, it doesn't even matter how the policy is represented. It does its hocus pocus, you sample it, and you average the returns. So why keep theta around? Because the other half of the system, the actor, needs it. The actor is the one doing policy learning. You can go one step further and bootstrap: use the reward plus the next state's value, instead of the full return. Even less variance, at the price of a little bias.

41.title: Actor critic
41.text: Put them together: actor critic. The critic updates its weights w by TD. The actor updates theta by a policy gradient. Take an action from the policy. See the reward and the next state. Compute the TD error: reward, plus gamma times the next value, minus the current value. The critic moves its value toward the target, exactly like TD zero. That part is value-based learning, the same as always. The actor moves theta by the same TD error, times the gradient of log pi. If the action turned out better than expected, do it more often.

41.title: Everything moves
41.text: And it's a loop. A new theta changes which actions we sample. That changes the states and rewards we see. That changes the TD error. Which changes both updates. Everything moves at once. Like Sarsa, in spirit. A bit dizzying, and in practice, it's what most modern reinforcement learning uses. If one of them moves too fast, the other is chasing a moving target. So usually the critic learns a bit faster than the actor.

41.title: Our corridor runs
41.text: Back to the short corridor. Same start, a poor policy. A hundred runs, a thousand episodes, three methods. REINFORCE on its own: twenty three steps per episode at the start, thirteen point four by the end. With a learned baseline: seventeen and a half at the start, eleven point nine by the end. One-step actor critic: fourteen point six at the start, eleven point nine by the end. The critic helps most early on, when the policy is still bad. A fair warning: each method has its own step sizes, and we didn't tune them to the bone. The ordering is the point, not the decimals.

41.title: Trust regions
41.text: One more danger. In supervised learning, the data doesn't care about your model. Here, a bad policy collects bad data. Not wrong data. It's part of the dynamics, it has every right to exist. It just doesn't help you. So we don't want to step too far. A popular idea: limit how much the policy changes between updates, measured by the KL divergence, a distance between distributions. Maximise J, minus some penalty times that divergence. That's the idea behind trust region methods like TRPO and PPO. Our run: a three armed bandit. With a step size of five, almost a quarter of the runs had locked onto a worse arm by the end. With point two, none did. Big steps learn fast when they're right, and badly when they're wrong. A trust region is a seat belt.

41.title: Recap
41.text: So: the critic learns values, the actor learns the policy, and the TD error connects them. Keep the steps small enough that bad data can't take over. And remember, there are many variants. The papers are cute and readable. Chef's recommendation. Next time: what happens when there are infinitely many actions?

42.title: A car picks a speed
42.text: Picture an autonomous car. The action: how fast to drive, anywhere between zero and a hundred. That's a continuous action. Infinitely many choices. And for value-based methods, that's a headache. How do you even store q for every speed? And how do you find the maximum over infinitely many actions, at every single step? Philosophically, by the way, no engine gives you an infinitely fine throttle. In practice, everything is discrete. But it's continuous enough to hurt. Why not just discretise? Zero to a hundred in steps of one is a hundred and one actions. Now add steering, and braking. It explodes quickly.

42.title: A distribution over speeds
42.text: With policy gradients, continuous actions are much easier. The policy just has to output a distribution over speeds. Careful with words: the policy isn't Gaussian. It's a function. The distribution it returns over actions can be. So say the action is drawn from a normal distribution, with a mean mu that depends on the state, and a fixed spread, sigma. And here's the cheat. A gradient over an infinite set of actions just became a gradient over two numbers. Mu and sigma. How do you feel about infinite vectors? Not fun. Vectors of size two? Much better. So instead of a value for every possible speed, we learn where to aim, and how much to wobble around it.

42.title: The Gaussian gradient
42.text: For a Gaussian, the gradient of log pi is simple: the action minus the mean, divided by sigma squared, times the gradient of the mean. Plug that into REINFORCE with a baseline. If the return was better than expected, move the mean toward the action you just tried. If it was worse, move the mean away. The exploration comes for free, from the spread. And sigma can be learned too. Start wide, explore a lot, and narrow down as you become more confident.

42.title: Our speed toy
42.text: A toy run. The car must pick a speed, and somewhere there's a best speed, sixty three. The closer, the better the reward. The car doesn't know any of this. It starts with a mean of twenty and a spread of ten. Two hundred runs. After about three hundred tries, the average mean is within two of sixty three. By the end, it sits right on it.

42.title: Approximately right
42.text: The price: we assumed the distribution has a nice parametric shape. That's usually not exactly true. Approximately true, often. If you noticed, this course started perfect. Everything with proofs. And then it went downhill. Approximately here, roughly there. A student once told me it's like cooking or painting. It doesn't need to be perfect. I'm a mathematician. Mathematics is the only profession where things are perfect. We live in a purer world. In practice, you compare against the state of the art, not against the theoretical optimum. Unless you're a student in my lab. Then you compare against the theoretical optimum. Just kidding. A model that's right ninety percent of the time, or one that's right ninety five percent? You take the ninety five, even though both are sometimes wrong.

42.title: Climb q
42.text: Policy gradients don't lean on the critic very much. If values generalise well, maybe we can lean on them more. Learn q with something like Sarsa. Let the actor output one action, deterministically. Then move the actor up the slope of q, in the direction of better actions. This idea has had many names over the years. Today it's mostly known as the deterministic policy gradient. And it's a form of policy iteration again.

42.title: Cacla
42.text: One more, and I like it a lot: Cacla. The continuous actor critic learning automaton. It measures the error in action space, not in parameter space. The actor proposes an action. You explore around it, and try a slightly different one. The critic computes the TD error, and updates its value as usual. If the TD error is positive, move the actor toward the action you tried. If it's zero or negative, don't touch the actor at all. Two nice things. It never pushes away from bad actions. And the size of the update doesn't depend on how big the rewards are. If the try was worse, you don't really know which direction is better. So Cacla does nothing, and waits for a good surprise.

42.title: The queen, ×100
42.text: Why not push away from bad actions? Chess. Sometimes you sacrifice your queen, and a few moves later, you checkmate. Losing the queen looks terrible right away. With Cacla, that moment doesn't teach the actor anything. The win afterwards does. So it doesn't learn never sacrifice a queen. It learns sacrifice, then mate, is a good idea. We tested the second property on our speed toy. Multiply every reward by a hundred, and keep the step size. The Gaussian policy gradient blew up in all two hundred runs. Cacla didn't even notice: the same three hundred tries to reach sixty three.

42.title: Module ten, done
42.text: That's module ten. Learn the policy directly. Climb the gradient with the score function trick, and calm the noise with a baseline and a critic. Keep your steps small. And when actions are continuous, let a distribution do the exploring, or let Cacla follow the good surprises. Next module: learning about many things at once. General value functions.

43.title: One number, a narrow picture
43.text: Module eleven: learning about many things. So far, our agents chased one number. One reward, one value, one policy. And a narrow goal gives you a narrow picture of the world. A narrow representation can't support good generalisation. The deadly triad and value leakage only make it worse. Think of a ship. If the only thing you ever practised is sailing in a straight line, you'll be lost the day someone asks for a circle. Better: first learn how a ship moves. Then a straight line, a circle, whatever you're asked. Rich knowledge first.

43.title: Knowledge as predictions
43.text: Remember the reward hypothesis, from the very first lecture? Any goal can be written as maximising a scalar reward. Push it one step further. Maybe all useful knowledge can be written as predictions. Not just about reward. About anything. That's a general value function. Sutton and colleagues, two thousand eleven. Swap the reward for a cumulant, c: any signal you care about. And make two more things flexible. The discount, gamma, can depend on the state. And the policy can be any policy, even a hypothetical one. You've noticed, I'm sure. This course started very mathematical, and slowly became more and more engineering. This is engineering.

43.title: Turning the knobs
43.text: Let's play with the knobs. Cumulant equals reward, under my own policy, with my usual gamma. That's plain policy evaluation. Nothing new. Cumulant equals reward, and gamma equals zero. Now I only predict the very next reward. Which object did that, earlier in the course? The model. Cumulant equals the next state, or a feature of it, with gamma zero. Given a state and an action, predict where you land. That's the dynamics. Same architecture, same learning rule. Just different questions. You get all of these as a gift, by turning a few knobs. And the policy knob: what would happen if I always walked left? You can learn that answer without ever walking left. That's off-policy learning, and we'll meet it again as an open problem.

43.title: A discount per state
43.text: Why would gamma depend on the state? Think chess. At the start of the game, how far do you want to look? Far. The game is long. Near the end, you want to finish the job. A short horizon. So a gamma that depends on the state can make sense. And a gamma of zero in some states means: this question ends here. Discount and termination are the same knob. Choose it wisely, and it helps. Choose it badly, and it hurts. And as usual, you mostly find out which one afterwards.

43.title: Our corridor, three questions
43.text: We tried it. A corridor of seven cells, an agent walking at random. One stream of experience, and three questions learned at the same time. Question one: how much reward is coming, from the right end of the corridor? Gamma point nine. Question two: will I touch the left wall on the very next step? Gamma zero. Question three: how soon will I reach it? Gamma point eight. Twenty thousand steps of plain TD learning, for all three at once. All three ended with an average error below a tenth. Two of them, far below. None of these questions is the task. But together, they say a lot about where the agent is.

43.title: Sub-goals, and a boxing story
43.text: Cumulants are also a way to add sub-goals. Back to the ship. The main reward: sail in a straight line. Add a few more signals. Don't capsize. Here's a good idea: stop capsizing. And if you sail in a zigzag, fine by me, I'm still happy. A story I like. Two simulated agents, trained to box against each other. One of them found a brilliant move: fall to the floor, and do nothing. The other one had never seen anything like it. It had no idea what to do, and it fell apart. The one lying on the floor won. The fix was a new signal: if you fall on the floor, I'm angry with you. A small cumulant, a very different agent.

43.title: Train on one, judge on another
43.text: Which brings an important habit. Agents are often trained on one reward, and evaluated on another. In the boxing example, when we evaluate, we only care who wins. Falling or not falling doesn't matter there. Usually the evaluation reward sits inside the training reward. You still want to train in the right direction. The extras are there to help, not to replace.

43.title: Predictions as the state
43.text: Now a bold idea, from predictive state representations. Littman, Sutton and Singh, two thousand two. Ask a large and diverse set of questions. If the set is rich enough, the answers say everything you need about the state. So use the predictions themselves as the state. Then learn the policy and the values as a simple, linear function of those predictions. Our corridor already shows the spirit. Will I touch the wall now? How soon? How much reward is coming? Three answers, and you can roughly tell where you are, without anyone telling you. Your state is no longer what you see. It's what you expect to happen.

43.title: Recap
43.text: So: a general value function predicts any cumulant, with any discount, under any policy. Reward prediction, dynamics, policy evaluation: all special cases. And asking many questions builds a richer picture of the world. Next time: put many questions into one network, and let them teach each other. Auxiliary tasks.

44.title: One body, many heads
44.text: Last time, many questions. Today, one network that answers them all. Look at the networks we met in this course. What goes in? Always the state, or the state and an action. Nothing else makes sense. Could a network take only an action? What would it learn? Nothing. We never defined a useful function from an action alone. So the input is the same. What changes between a policy network, a value network, and a Q network? Only the last layer. The head. Which means you can keep one body, and give it many heads. A multi-head network. Training is simple: add up the losses, maybe with a weight on each. And every weight is one more knob to tune.

44.title: Auxiliary tasks
44.text: That's the idea of auxiliary tasks, from Jaderberg and colleagues, two thousand sixteen. General value functions, as extra heads on a shared network. You minimise the main loss and the auxiliary losses together. You don't really care about the auxiliary answers. You care about what they do to the shared layers. They make the representation richer and more robust. You can even let the auxiliary losses train only the representation, and leave the layers above it alone.

44.title: Capture the flag
44.text: An example. Capture the flag. Find the other team's flag, and bring it home. The reward: win the game. Mathematically, if you work long enough, you'll find a good policy. Let me make it easier for the network. Add a task: find the flag. And another: when you have the flag, get back to base. Sub-tasks of winning, in the right order. I don't care much about either of them on their own. But on the way, the network learns a representation that serves all of them. And winning gets easier. These extra signals are called pseudo-rewards. Pseudo, not sudo. Nothing to do with Linux. That was a great joke, by the way.

44.title: Pixels, features, rewards
44.text: Two classic auxiliary tasks. Pixel control: learn to change the pixels on the screen as much as possible. Picture the screen cut into a grid of small squares. For each square, one question: which actions change this square the most? Lots of questions, and the screen answers them for free. Feature control: the same idea, but for the network's own hidden features. Learn to change them as much as possible. And reward prediction: from three recent frames, guess whether the next reward is positive, negative, or zero. Rewards are rare, so rewarding moments are replayed more often, about half the time. None of these is the game. All of them force the network to understand what it can change in its

44.title: Does it work?
44.text: world. Does it work? In their paper, on a suite of three D maze tasks called Labyrinth, the plain agent averaged fifty four percent of expert human performance. With all the auxiliary tasks together: eighty seven percent. And it learned about ten times faster on average. Same main reward. Same data. More questions on the side. And the extra rewards are only for learning. The agent is still judged on the game score alone.

44.title: The honest part
44.text: Now the honest part. Ask an engineer: what happens when a machine has more moving parts? More chances that one of them breaks. Every extra task can help, and every extra task is another point of failure. And not every task helps. Add a task called have a picnic, and the network will learn something about picnics. It won't help you capture the flag. Which tasks help? Like many things in this course: you try, you find out you were wrong, you try again. You only know afterwards. Partly because we, the world, not just this class, don't fully understand how neural networks work. We understand fully connected networks better every year. And we're already at transformers. And not every good idea is the newest. One of my favourites is the clockwork network: parts of its memory tick at different speeds, some every step, some only every few steps. Cheaper than an LSTM, and in my experience, great for physics, where signals have a rhythm.

44.title: The value improvement path
44.text: One more angle: the value improvement path. Dabney and colleagues, twenty twenty. While learning, the agent's policy keeps improving. So the network must represent a whole sequence of value functions, from the first poor policy to the best one. A good representation supports the entire path, not just the end. Auxiliary tasks can help keep it flexible along the way. A related idea: tasks that build on each other. Think of a game with levels. Win level one. Then levels one and two. Then one, two and three. A student suggested a nicer one: teach a language model a sentence, then a paragraph, then a whole article. Each task extends the one before.

44.title: Toolbox or staircase
44.text: The difference matters. Before, the extra tasks were just a list. If they happened to help each other, great. Here, each task deliberately extends the previous one, on the way to the final task. Your teacher builds the ladder, one rung at a time. The first is a toolbox. The second is a staircase.

44.title: Recap
44.text: So: one body, many heads. The heads ask extra questions. The body gets a better picture of the world. Choose the questions with care, and expect some trial and error. Next time: what happens when one task shouts much louder than the others?

45.title: Tasks compete
45.text: We want to learn as much as possible about the world. But capacity and compute are limited. And different tasks compete for them. There's always a trade-off. Even if you do nothing explicit about it, you've made a choice. The size of each task's updates to the shared weights grows with how big and how frequent its rewards are. A loud task pulls the representation its way. So some tasks shape the shared layers a lot, and some barely at all. Not because they matter more. Just because their numbers are bigger. A classic fix: the DQN agent on Atari clipped every reward to between minus one and one. Simple, and it keeps the scales tame. But in some games, a small pellet is worth ten points, and catching a ghost is worth hundreds. After clipping, both are plus one. The scale is fixed, and the task has quietly changed.

45.title: No full dataset
45.text: In supervised learning, you know the dataset in advance. So you normalise inputs and targets to sensible scales. Many deep models barely work without that. In reinforcement learning, you don't have the full dataset. Worse, the scale of the values you predict keeps changing as the agent improves. So the normalisation has to adapt, while you learn.

45.title: Normalise while you learn
45.text: Adaptive target normalisation, from van Hasselt and colleagues, twenty sixteen. Step one: see a target, like a Q-learning target. Step two: update a running mean of the targets, and a running average of their squares. That gives you a running variance, too. Step three: the network predicts the target minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation. Statisticians call that a z-score. Say the targets so far average a thousand, with a spread of a hundred. A target of eleven hundred becomes plus one. Nine hundred becomes minus one. Every task now speaks at the same volume. Step four: whenever you need the real value, for example to bootstrap, multiply back by the standard deviation and add the mean. These running estimates are approximations, and not great ones early on. But they fix the problem of scale.

45.title: Preserve the outputs
45.text: One catch. Every time the normalisation changes, every output of the network changes too. Even for states you never touched. That seems bad. We shouldn't change the values of unrelated states. The fix is neat. When the mean and the standard deviation move, rescale the last layer's weights and bias by exactly the opposite amount. The real outputs stay put. That's the name: PopArt. Preserving outputs precisely, while adaptively rescaling targets.

45.title: Our toy run
45.text: Our toy run. Two prediction tasks share one hidden layer. One target lives around one. The other around a thousand. Plain stochastic gradient descent, at the step size that suits the big task: the big task ends within ten percent. The small one stays at eighty three percent error. Drowned out. We tried five step sizes. The best compromise left both tasks above thirty percent error. With PopArt-style normalisation, one step size: both tasks end within about ten percent. The same idea, with one normalisation per game, let a single agent learn all fifty seven Atari games at once. Hessel and colleagues, twenty nineteen. One set of weights, above the median human score.

45.title: Open: off-policy
45.text: Now some open problems. If you want to write papers in this area, here are some questions. Some have been open for years. Off-policy learning. Can we learn about one cumulant while following a policy that maximises a different one? In one paper, called Unicorn, the agent must pick up a key, then a lock, then a door, then a chest, in that order. An agent trained only for the chest never did better than random. Learning about every step of the chain together, off-policy, from the same experience, got there. Learn about many things, to do the hard thing. Splitting a goal into sub-tasks is easy when you know the policy that collected the data. Off-policy, it's much less clear how.

45.title: Open: universal value functions
45.text: Generalisation. So far, each general value function is learned on its own. Can what we learn about one question help with another? One idea: feed the question itself into the network as an input. The cumulant, the discount. Then the network can generalise across goals. And since the name general value function was already taken, these were called universal value functions. Schaul and colleagues, twenty fifteen. Think of a maze where the goal can be anywhere. Train on some goal positions, and the network can make a sensible guess for a goal it has never trained on.

45.title: Open: discovery
45.text: And discovery. Which questions should an agent ask? Instead of choosing them by hand, learn them from experience, with meta-learning. Meta-learning means learning how to learn. A classic example: give a model a table, and let it tell you which learning algorithm will work best on it. It's a field I love. My own little corner is meta-learning for feature selection. Everyone needs their own little corner.

45.title: Recap
45.text: So: tasks compete, whether you like it or not. Normalise targets so no task drowns the others, and preserve the outputs while you do it. And the open questions: learning off-policy, generalising across questions, and discovering which questions to ask. Next time: stop predicting one number. Predict the whole distribution.

46.title: One number hides the shape
46.text: Everything so far predicted an expectation. One number: the average return. But the return is random. Roll a die. The average is three and a half. You will never, ever roll a three and a half. Remember the world from module nine? Minus a million once, plus a million once, and zero all the other times. The expectation is zero. Exactly like a world where nothing ever happens. Same average, very different worlds. One of them, you'd like to know about in advance. Same with the weather. Two millimetres of rain on average tells you less than: eighty percent dry, twenty percent storm.

46.title: The whole distribution
46.text: Distributional reinforcement learning: learn the whole distribution of returns, not just its mean. The value function takes a state, and instead of one number, it gives back a distribution of possible returns. A richer learning signal. And that can help the network learn more robust representations, the same story as auxiliary tasks. And there's a Bellman equation for it, too. The return is the reward, plus gamma times the next return. Not as averages this time, but as random variables, distribution and all.

46.title: The catch
46.text: What's the catch? It's harder. We have endless tools to predict a number: regression, classification, you name it. We, the world, are much less good at predicting distributions. There are tools, but far fewer, and they're harder to use. Regression gives you a number, maybe with an error bar. A full shape, with two humps, or a long tail? That's much harder.

46.title: C51: a comb
46.text: One way to do it: Categorical DQN, from Bellemare and colleagues, twenty seventeen. Fix a comb of possible returns. Say, fifty one points between minus ten and ten. For each point, the network outputs a probability. The distribution is the comb with those probabilities. To act, you still use the mean: each point times its probability, summed up. Fifty one points, a categorical distribution. That's why people call it C51.

46.title: Shift, shrink, project
46.text: Learning it looks like Q-learning, with a twist. Take the next state's distribution, for its best action. Shift it by the reward, and shrink it by gamma. Now the points don't sit on your comb anymore. So project them back onto the comb, splitting each point's probability between its two nearest neighbours. A tiny example. Say the comb has a point at every whole number. Reward one, gamma point nine, and a point sitting at five. It moves to five and a half. So half its probability goes to five, and half goes to six. Then make your current distribution closer to that target, by minimising the KL divergence. In practice, a cross-entropy loss.

46.title: Our die and coin
46.text: Our run. A one-step world: roll a die, get the number, game over. Fifty one points, a categorical learner, nothing else. It puts about one sixth of the probability near each face, one to six. Its mean: three point four five. The truth: three point five. Close, not perfect. It's still a learner, with a finite number of samples. Now a coin: plus ten or minus ten. Two clear spikes at the ends, nothing in the middle. The mean is about zero, but the picture says something completely different.

46.title: Quantiles
46.text: There are many other ways to model the distribution. Quantile regression, from Dabney and colleagues, flips the idea around. Instead of fixed points with learned probabilities, fix the probabilities and learn where the points go. Eleven quantiles, say, each one owning the same share of the probability. How does each point find its place? Take the point for the bottom ten percent. When a sample lands above it, nudge it up a little. When one lands below, nudge it down a lot. It settles where one sample in ten falls below it. On our die, most of the eleven points land right on the faces: two at one, two at two, one at three, and so on. A few are still on their way between faces. On the coin, five land at minus ten, five land at plus ten, and the middle one wanders somewhere in between. With a coin, that's honest.

46.title: Why bother
46.text: Why bother, if we act on the mean anyway? First, the richer signal shapes better representations. Second, you can see risk. Two actions with the same mean, one of them occasionally catastrophic. Now you can tell them apart. Two routes to work. One takes thirty minutes, every day. The other takes twenty five, but one day in five, it takes fifty. Same average. If you have a flight to catch, you know which one you want. Remember the bandit with a million dollar jackpot, and a hundred dollars in your pocket? The distribution is what tells you to walk away. Third, an agent can use the distribution to be careful: avoid actions with a long, bad tail, even when their average looks fine. And a beautiful twist. In twenty twenty, Dabney and colleagues found evidence for this in mice. Different dopamine neurons seem more optimistic or more pessimistic, and together they encode a whole distribution of rewards.

46.title: Module eleven, done
46.text: That's module eleven. Ask many questions, with general value functions. Share one network, with auxiliary tasks. Keep the loud tasks from drowning the quiet ones, with PopArt. And when one number isn't enough, learn the whole distribution. Next module: learning from humans. Demonstrations, preferences, and how language models got their manners.

47.title: Write a reward for driving
47.text: Module twelve, the last one: learning from humans. Let's start with a challenge. Write me a reward for driving well. Go on, I'll wait. Stay in the lane. Don't hit anything. Don't brake too hard. Be polite at roundabouts. Every rule you add, an agent will find a loophole in. But any decent driver can just show you. One drive, and you see more than ten pages of rules.

47.title: Imitation learning
47.text: That's imitation learning. It's useful when demonstrating the behaviour is easier than writing the reward, or writing the policy directly. Driving. Tying a surgical knot. Folding a shirt. Ask an expert for a formula, and you get a shrug. Ask them to do it, and you get a demonstration. So the input changes. We still have states and actions. Sometimes we know the dynamics, sometimes not. But there is no reward at all. Instead, we get demonstrations: sequences of states and actions, from an expert's policy, pi star.

47.title: Three questions
47.text: From there, three questions. First, behaviour cloning: can we learn the expert's policy directly, with supervised learning? Second, inverse reinforcement learning: can we recover the reward the expert was optimising? Third, apprenticeship learning: can we use that reward to find a good policy of our own?

47.title: Behaviour cloning
47.text: Behaviour cloning first, because it's the simplest. Every state the expert visited is an input. The action they took is the label. Train a classifier. Done. This is the moment in the course where the supervised learning people finally relax. And it doesn't need the dynamics model. You never ask what happens next. You only ask what the expert did here. Mathematically: take every state and action pair from the demonstrations, and minimise the usual classification loss. Nothing in it knows about time. It works surprisingly often. And it fails in a very specific, very sneaky way.

47.title: Compounding errors
47.text: The expert is good. So the expert almost never makes mistakes. Which means the data never shows how to recover from one. Imagine learning to drive only from videos of perfect drivers. You've never seen anyone fix a drift. So the first time you drift, you're on your own. The copy makes one small error, and lands in a state the expert never visited. There, it has no idea what to do, so it makes a bigger error. And another. In supervised learning, the test data comes from the same place as the training data. Here, the copy chooses its own test data, by driving. People call this compounding errors, or distribution shift. A tiny error rate per step can add up to a big mess over a long drive.

47.title: Our lane toy
47.text: We tried it. A road nine cells wide. Gusts of wind push the car left or right, fifteen percent of the time each. The expert always steers back toward the centre. In twenty demonstrations, it never left the middle three cells. Our copy follows a table built from those demonstrations. But five percent of the time it picks a random action. And where it has no data at all, it acts at random. Two thousand drives of two hundred steps each. The expert went off the road zero times. The copy, in thirty seven percent of the drives. And look where the copy spent its last moments: in cells the expert never visited, with nothing to copy.

47.title: DAgger
47.text: The fix has a nice name: DAgger. Dataset aggregation, Ross, Gordon and Bagnell, twenty eleven. Let the copy drive. Every state it visits, ask the expert: what would you have done here? Add those answers to the data, and train again. Now the data includes the copy's own mistakes, with the right correction attached. In our toy, after one round, the copy went off the road in two drives out of a thousand. Ross and colleagues also showed why it matters. For behaviour cloning, the cost of small mistakes can grow with the square of the horizon. With DAgger, roughly linearly. The price: the expert has to sit in the passenger seat, for every round. Experts are expensive, and they get bored.

47.title: Inverse RL
47.text: Inverse reinforcement learning takes the other road. Don't copy the actions. Figure out what the expert wanted. Why? A reward transfers. New car, new road, new weather: the actions change, but the goal of not dying stays the same. A classic idea is feature matching, from Abbeel and Ng, two thousand four. Describe each state with features: speed, distance to the car ahead, lane position. If your policy visits those features as often as the expert does, you earn about the same reward. For any reward built from those features, with bounded weights. But there's a catch. Infinitely many rewards share the same optimal policy. Give zero reward everywhere, and every policy is optimal. Which reward should we pick? And the third question, apprenticeship learning, is the easy part. Once you have a reward, any method from this course can find a policy for

47.title: Recap
47.text: it. So: imitation learning, for when showing is easier than explaining. Behaviour cloning is simple, but it drifts. DAgger fixes the drift, at the price of a patient expert. Inverse RL looks for the reward instead. Next time: of all the rewards that could explain the expert, pick the least surprised one. Maximum entropy.

48.title: Many rewards, one principle
48.text: Last time, a problem. Many rewards explain the same expert. We need a principle to pick one. Here's one, from Edwin Jaynes, nineteen fifty seven. The principle of maximum entropy. Among all the distributions that agree with what you know, pick the one with the largest entropy. Commit to nothing you don't actually know. Think of a detective with too many suspects. You need a rule for choosing, or you end up accusing

48.title: Entropy
48.text: everybody. Entropy, quickly. Minus the sum of p times log p. It measures how spread out, how uncommitted, a distribution is. Someone hands you a die and tells you nothing. What's your honest guess? One sixth for each face. That's the maximum entropy distribution. Any other guess says: I know something about this die. And you don't. Claiming knowledge you don't have is how you lose money at the market. A coin that always lands heads has entropy zero. No surprise at all. A fair coin has the most entropy a coin can have.

48.title: A loaded die
48.text: Now add one fact. The average roll of this die is four and a half. Not three and a half. So it's loaded. But how, exactly? Many distributions have that average. Maximum entropy picks one, and its shape is always the same: exponential in the face value. We computed it. Five percent for a one, eight for a two, eleven, seventeen, twenty four, and thirty five percent for a six. Tilted, but nothing ruled out. Why not put all the weight on fours and fives? Because nothing told you a one is impossible. Maximum entropy only bends as far as the facts force

48.title: Trajectories
48.text: it to. Ziebart and colleagues, two thousand eight, did the same for trajectories. What we know: the expert's demonstrations, summarised by their features. The maximum entropy answer: the probability of a trajectory is proportional to e to the power of its reward. Better trajectories are exponentially more likely. But no trajectory is impossible. The expert is assumed to be good, and a little noisy. Just like real experts. Remember softmax policies from module ten? Same exponential, one level up. Over whole trajectories, instead of single actions. Two paths with the same reward get the same probability. The expert has no favourite between them, so neither do we.

48.title: The gradient
48.text: How do we find the reward? Make the demonstrations as likely as possible under this distribution. Maximum likelihood. For a linear reward, that's the same problem as maximum entropy, constrained to match the expert's feature counts. Two roads, one answer. And the gradient is beautiful. How often the expert visits each state, minus how often my current policy visits it. More of what the expert does. Less of what I do and the expert doesn't. I wish my own habits had a gradient this simple. Notice what the gradient doesn't need: the expert's exact actions. Only where the expert went, and how often.

48.title: The algorithm
48.text: The algorithm, then. Start with some reward. Compute the best soft policy for it, for example with value iteration. Compute how often that policy visits each state. Take one gradient step on the reward. Repeat. A check for you: which steps need the dynamics model? Computing the policy, and computing the visit frequencies. Behaviour cloning, remember, needed neither. In a big world, computing those visit frequencies exactly is expensive. That's one reason later methods sample instead.

48.title: Our grid
48.text: Our run. A five by five grid, a goal in one corner, and a small lake of lava in the middle. Thirty demonstrations from an expert that walks around it. The learner sees only the paths. Nobody tells it about the lava. It learns one reward per cell. Three hundred updates. The gap between its visit counts and the expert's shrank from fifteen point six to zero point one eight. Its policy reaches the goal in almost every run. It still steps on lava in about five percent of runs, because a maximum entropy policy stays a little noisy. The expert never did. And the learned reward? It looks like the true one, but not exactly. A correlation of about point eight. Many rewards explain the same paths, remember.

48.title: Beyond
48.text: The original method assumed two things: a reward that's linear in the features, and a known dynamics model. Finn and colleagues, twenty sixteen, removed both. General reward functions, learned while the robot acts, without knowing the dynamics in advance. And Ho and Ermon, twenty sixteen, went further: generative adversarial imitation learning. A critic tries to tell the expert from the learner. The learner tries to fool it. It's a lot like the adversarial networks that generate fake photos. Only here, the fakes are behaviour. Imitation can cut the data you need by a lot. And combining it with online reinforcement learning is still a very open, very exciting area.

48.title: Recap
48.text: So: when many rewards fit, pick the least committed distribution that still matches the expert. Trajectories become exponentially likely in their reward. The gradient matches visit counts. And the learned reward explains the behaviour, without being unique. Next time: what if the human doesn't demonstrate at all? What if they just say which of two things they like better?

49.title: Kinds of feedback
49.text: Humans can help an agent learn in many ways. Demonstrations are only one of them. A person can hand out rewards while the agent acts, like a clicker for a dog. Knox and Stone's TAMER framework learns a model of those human rewards. Thomaz and Breazeal, two thousand eight, watched people teach a robot. People didn't only reward the past. They used rewards to guide what the robot should do next. People can also correct an action, give advice, or compare two attempts. Each kind of feedback costs a different amount of human effort. Each kind also carries different information. A demonstration shows what to do. A correction shows what not to do, and what instead. A comparison only says: better, or worse.

49.title: The effort line
49.text: Put them on a line. At one end, constant teaching, like DAgger: an expert labels everything the agent does, round after round. At the other end, demonstrations only. The expert shows a few examples, and goes home. Somewhere in between: pairwise labels. Show the person two things, and ask which one is better. Maybe that's the sweet spot. And remember: the more effort each label costs, the fewer labels you'll get. Experts have day jobs.

49.title: Why pairs
49.text: Why pairs? Try this. How much do you like this advertisement, on a scale from one to ten? Ask me to rate a pizza from one to ten, I'll say seven. Every pizza is a seven. Put two pizzas in front of me, and suddenly I have very strong opinions. Absolute ratings are noisy, and every person uses the scale differently. Comparisons are easier to give, and much more consistent. Another bonus: comparisons don't care whether someone is generous or strict with numbers. Everybody's better means better.

49.title: Bradley–Terry
49.text: To learn from comparisons, we need a model of how people choose. The classic is Bradley and Terry, nineteen fifty two. Every option has a hidden score, r. To get the probability that a person prefers option i over option j, raise e to each score, and take i's share of the total. Equivalently, a sigmoid of the difference in scores. Same family as the softmax, again. Equal scores: a coin flip. A big gap: almost always the better one. Two consequences. Only differences matter, so add the same number to every score and nothing changes. And the model is transitive: one score per option means a clean ranking. Think of chess ratings. The rating difference between two players tells you how likely one is to beat the other. Same spirit.

49.title: Who wins?
49.text: What does it mean to win, with noisy comparisons? There are a few answers. A Condorcet winner beats every other option more than half the time. A Copeland winner has the most head-to-head wins. A Borda winner has the best average score against everyone. In a Bradley-Terry world, the option with the highest score is all three at once. Real preferences don't always cooperate. We'll see why in a minute. Which winner do we want? It depends on the application. Historically, algorithms for dueling bandits mostly looked for the Copeland winner.

49.title: Fitting the scores
49.text: Fitting the scores is just maximum likelihood. Each comparison is a small classification problem: did i win, or did j? The loss is the cross-entropy between what the person said and what the model predicted. Logistic regression, on differences in scores. With enough comparisons, of enough different pairs, the fitted scores approach the hidden ones. Two options that are never connected by any chain of comparisons? Their gap can't be learned. Each comparison nudges the winner's score up and the loser's down. More when the result was a surprise, less when it was expected.

49.title: Our five options
49.text: Our run. Five options, with hidden scores. A simulated person compares random pairs, and picks according to Bradley and Terry. After twenty comparisons, the fitted ranking is wrong.
