The best option isn't even on top. Twenty noisy answers are not much. After two hundred, the ranking is exactly right. After two thousand, the fitted scores are close to the hidden ones. The largest error, on the top option, is about a tenth of a point.

49.title: A cycle
49.text: Now a person with a cycle. Rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, paper beats rock. Each preference holds ninety percent of the time. We fitted Bradley and Terry to twelve hundred of these comparisons. All three scores came out at about zero. So the model predicts a coin flip for every pair. The truth is ninety ten, every time. One score per option simply can't hold a cycle. Do real people have cycles? Ask anyone choosing a restaurant with friends. And it gets worse when you combine many people's preferences. Hold that thought for the last episode.

49.title: Recap
49.text: So: humans can help in many ways, at different costs. Pairwise comparisons are cheap and consistent, and Bradley and Terry turn them into scores. The same idea works for whole trajectories. The score of a trajectory is the sum of its rewards. Ask which of two trajectories is better, and fit the rewards. That gives us a reward model, learned from comparisons. And once you have a reward model, you know what to do next. Next time: reinforcement learning from human feedback. From robots doing backflips, to chatbots.

50.title: A reward model
50.text: Last time, we learned a reward model from comparisons. Now let's use it. Two trajectories. Each has a sum of rewards that nobody wrote down. The probability that a person prefers the first is a sigmoid of the difference between the two sums. Fit the reward model so it agrees with the people. Then forget about the people for a moment, and run reinforcement learning on the learned reward. For example, with PPO. In other words: the people teach the reward model, and the reward model teaches the agent. The agent never talks to a person directly.

50.title: The backflip
50.text: The classic demonstration: Christiano and colleagues, twenty seventeen. A simulated robot learns to do a backflip. Try writing a reward for a backflip. Height? Rotation speed? Landing on your feet, not your face? Good luck. Instead, a person watched pairs of short clips and picked the one that looked more like a backflip. About nine hundred pieces of feedback, and the robot flipped. The robot didn't need to understand backflips. It needed a reward model that agreed with the person often enough. Nine hundred clicks. I've spent more clicks choosing a laptop.

50.title: Three stages
50.text: Now the famous one: language models. The recipe has three stages. Stage one: pretrain a big model to predict the next word, on a lot of text. Stage two: instruction tuning. Fine-tune it on demonstrations of good answers. Stage three: collect comparisons. The model writes several answers to the same prompt, and people rank them. Fit a reward model. Then optimise the language model against it. Notice the old friends. Stage two is behaviour cloning. Stage three is Bradley and Terry, and then a policy gradient method. And stage one alone gives you a model that continues text. Ask it a question, and it might answer with three more questions.

50.title: The reward model
50.text: Why rank answers instead of scoring them? Because human judgements are noisy and miscalibrated. One person's seven is another person's four. The loss: minus the log of the sigmoid of the winner's reward minus the loser's. Push the winner up, push the loser down. And a piece of advice from the summarisation work of Stiennon and colleagues, twenty twenty: make sure your reward model works first. Test it on held-out human judgements. In their experiments, a large enough reward model, trained on enough comparisons, approached the agreement of a single human labeller. The reward model itself is often a copy of the language model, with a new head that outputs a single number.

50.title: On a leash
50.text: The RL step maximises the learned reward, minus beta times the log ratio between the new policy and the pretrained one. That second term is a price for wandering away from the original model. In expectation, it's the KL divergence between the two. Why pay that price? The reward model was trained on answers the original model writes. Far from those answers, nobody checked it. Keep beta in mind. Without it, the policy can drift into strange answers that the reward model happens to love. We'll see exactly that in a minute.

50.title: InstructGPT and ChatGPT
50.text: Does it work? In the InstructGPT paper, Ouyang and colleagues, twenty twenty two, labellers preferred the answers of a one point three billion parameter model trained this way. Over those of the hundred and seventy five billion parameter GPT-3. More than a hundred times smaller, and preferred. ChatGPT used the same recipe for dialogue. Many of the details, like the data and the model size, were never published. The same Bradley-Terry loss, the same policy gradients from module ten. Just at a much larger scale.

50.title: Our toy
50.text: We built a tiny version. Forty possible answers. A pretrained policy that mostly gives thirty ordinary answers, and only rarely gives ten strange ones. The strange ones sound extremely confident, and they're wrong. Our labeller only cares about quality. The reward model can't see quality directly. It sees how confident an answer sounds, plus a noisy hint of quality. On ordinary answers, confidence and quality go together. Three thousand comparisons later, it agrees with the labeller on eighty one percent of pairs. Not bad at all. So the reward model learned, sensibly: confident sounds good. On the answers it has seen, that's mostly true.

50.title: Pulling the leash
50.text: Now the RL step, with the KL price. With a large beta, the policy barely moves. As beta shrinks, it moves further. At first, everything is great. The learned reward goes up, and the true quality goes up with it, from minus point one eight to plus point two two. Push further. The learned reward keeps climbing, to one point eight seven. The true quality falls, to minus one. What happened? The policy found the confident, wrong answers, and now gives them every single time. The reward model loved them. Nobody had checked it there. On our toy, the best true quality came at a KL of about point eight. After that, every extra bit of optimisation made things worse.

50.title: Recap
50.text: So: RLHF learns a reward from human comparisons, and optimises against it, on a leash. It taught a robot to backflip, and a small model to beat a huge one in people's eyes. And pull the leash too hard, and it optimises the wrong thing. Next time, the last episode of the season: the limits of learning from humans.

51.title: Goodhart
51.text: The last episode of the season. Let's talk about what can go wrong. You saw it last time. Optimise a learned reward too hard, and the policy finds where the reward model is wrong. There's a popular version of Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. RLHF is a machine for turning measures into targets. For chatbots, the danger has a specific shape. A model rewarded for sounding authoritative and helpful can learn to sound that way regardless of the truth. And then it makes things up, confidently. We saw a cousin of this in module eleven, with the boxers. Reward the wrong thing, and agents get creative.

51.title: Unreliable preferences
51.text: Second problem: human preferences are unreliable. People get tired. People are rushed. People like longer answers, and nicer formatting. Dubois and colleagues, twenty twenty three, saw it clearly. After RLHF-style training, answers became much more detailed, with nicer, list-like formatting. Is a longer answer a better answer? Sometimes. Not always. And a model of human preferences is even less reliable than the humans themselves. Be honest: have you ever upvoted an answer because it looked thorough, without checking it? Long and wrong still looks impressive, at first glance.

51.title: Where labels come from
51.text: Third: where do the labels come from? Who are the labellers? How are they paid? What do they believe? The CS234 slides point out that labels often come from low-wage workers overseas. The quality and the fairness of that work both matter. And whose opinions end up in the model depends on who labelled the data. Santurkar and colleagues, twenty twenty three, asked exactly that: whose opinions do language models reflect? None of this is a reason to stop. It's a reason to report who labelled your data, and how, as carefully as you report your learning rate.

51.title: Condorcet's paradox
51.text: Now combine many people. Remember the cycle from two episodes ago? Here it comes back, without anyone being irrational. Three friends, three restaurants. The first ranks them A, B, C. The second goes B, C, A. And the third, C, A, B. Take a majority vote on each pair. A beats B. B beats C. C beats A. Three perfectly consistent people, and the group has a cycle. That's Condorcet's paradox. So learning from human preferences sits right where social choice, economics and AI meet. One reward model for everyone is a strong assumption. And when people genuinely disagree, a single reward model has to pick a side, or average them into something nobody actually wants.

51.title: Best-of-n
51.text: Fourth: is the full machinery even needed? Dubois and colleagues also found that simple baselines work well. One of them is best-of-n. Sample n answers from the model, and keep the one the reward model likes best. No reinforcement learning at all. On our toy from last time, best of eight was the sweet spot: true quality plus point six two. Best of a hundred and twenty eight: minus point nine. Same lesson, different tool. Search hard enough against a flawed reward, and you'll find its flaws. Best of n has a natural knob: n. Like beta, turn it up slowly, and keep checking with

51.title: DPO
51.text: real people. And there's a newer idea: direct preference optimisation, Rafailov and colleagues, twenty twenty three. Skip the separate reward model. Optimise the policy on the comparisons directly. It still learns from human preferences, so the questions about labels and labellers don't go away. Under the hood, DPO uses the same Bradley-Terry model and the same KL leash. It just solves for the policy more directly. Fewer moving parts. The same old question: whose preferences, and how carefully were they collected?

51.title: Three checks
51.text: Before we go, three quick checks, in the spirit of the CS234 quizzes. Does behaviour cloning need the dynamics model? No. It only maps states to actions. Does DAgger need more help from the expert after the demonstrations? Yes. Every round, the expert labels the states the learner visited. And in maximum entropy inverse RL, which steps need the dynamics? Computing the policy, and computing the visit frequencies. Three out of three? You were paying attention. If not, the episodes are still there. That's the nice thing about video.

51.title: The season
51.text: And that's the season. We started with a robot chasing one number: the reward hypothesis. Any goal, one scalar. Bandits and exploration. Markov decision processes, and dynamic programming. Learning from experience: Monte Carlo, and temporal differences. Then control. Function approximation, and deep networks. Planning, with models and search. Policy gradients, and actors with critics. Learning about many things at once. Twelve modules. Exactly one theorem, from Bellman. And a lot of engineering. And in this module, the humans write the number. Or rather, they whisper it, one comparison at a

51.title: Goodbye
51.text: time. So: learned rewards get hacked, human labels are noisy and come from real people, and groups of people don't always agree. None of that makes learning from humans a bad idea. It makes it a hard one. Which, in this course, usually means an interesting one. If you keep one slide from this whole course, keep the reward hypothesis. And the word I kept stressing: hypothesis. Thank you for learning with me this season. Now go write a good paper. And put me on it.
